author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A man must pay dear for his errors if he wishes to get rid of them, and even then he is lucky.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Enthusiasm is of the greatest value, so long as we are not carried away by it.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: School itself is the only true preparation for it.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Error is related to truth as sleep to waking. I have observed that on awakening from error a man turns again to truth as with new vigour.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Every one suffers who does not work for himself. A man works for others to have them share in his joy.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Men's prejudices rest upon their character for the time being and cannot be overcome, as being part and parcel of themselves. Neither evidence nor common-sense nor reason has the slightest influence upon them.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Characters often make a law of their failings. Men who know the world have said that when prudence is only fear in disguise, its scruples cannot be conquered. The weak often have revolutionary sentiments; they think they would be well off if they were not ruled, and fail to perceive that they can rule neither themselves nor others.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: All men, as they attain freedom, give play to their errors. The strong do too much, and the weak too little.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A great work limits us for the moment, because we feel it above our powers; and only in so far as we afterwards incorporate it with our culture, and make it part of our mind and heart, does it become a dear and worthy object.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is no wonder that we all more or less delight in the mediocre, because it leaves us in peace: it gives us the comfortable feeling of intercourse with what is like ourselves.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There is no use in reproving vulgarity, for it never changes.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: We cannot escape a contradiction in ourselves; we must try to resolve it. If the contradiction comes from others, it does not affect us: it is their affair.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There are many things in the world that are at once good and excellent, but they do not come into contact.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Which is the best government? That which teaches us to govern ourselves.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It may well be that a man is at times horribly threshed by misfortunes, public and private: but the reckless flail of Fate, when it beats the rich sheaves, crushes only the straw; and the corn feels nothing of it and dances merrily on the floor, careless whether its way is to the mill or the furrow.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: However probable it is that a desire may be fulfilled, there is always a doubt; and so when the desire is realised, it is always surprising.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Absurdities presented with good taste rouse disgust and admiration.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Of the best society it used to be said: their speech instructs the mind, and their silence the feelings.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Nothing is more terrible than ignorance in action.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Beauty and Genius must be kept afar if one would avoid becoming their slave.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: We treat the aged with consideration, as we treat children.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: An old man loses one of the greatest of human privileges: he is no more judged by his peers.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: In the matter of knowledge, it has happened to me as to one who rises early, and in the dark impatiently awaits the dawn, and then the sun; but is blinded when it appears.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Great primeval powers, evolved in time or in eternity, work on unceasingly: whether to weal or to woe, is a matter of chance.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Of the Absolute in the theoretical sense, I do not venture to speak; but this I maintain: that if a man recognises it in its manifestation, and always keeps his gaze fixed upon it, he will experience very great reward.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: To live in a great idea means to treat the impossible as though it were possible. It is just the same with a strong character; and when an idea and a character meet, things arise which fill the world with wonder for thousands of years.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: To the several perversities of the day a man should always oppose only the great masses of universal history.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: No one can live much with children without finding that they always react to any outward influence upon them.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: With any specially childish nature the reaction is even passionate, while its action is energetic.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: That is why children's lives are a series of refined judgments, not to say prejudices; and to efface a rapid but partial perception in order to make way for a more general one, time is necessary. To bear this in mind is one of the teacher's greatest duties.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Friendship can only be bred in practice and be maintained by practice. Affection, nay, love itself, is no help at all to friendship. True, active, productive friendship consists in keeping equal pace in life: in my friend approving my aims, while I approve his, and in thus moving forwards together steadfastly, however much our way of thought and life may vary.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: In the world people take a man at his own estimate; but he must estimate himself at something. Disagreeableness is more easily tolerated than insignificance.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: You can force anything on society so long as it has no sequel.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: We do not learn to know men if they come to us; we must go to them to find out what they are.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: That we have many criticisms to make on those who visit us, and that, as soon as they depart, we pass no very amiable judgment upon them, seems to me almost natural; for we have, so to speak, a right to measure them by our own standard. Even intelligent and fair-minded men hardly refrain from sharp censure on such occasions.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: What we call conduct and good manners obtains for us that which otherwise is to be obtained only by force, or not even by force.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: How can the character, the peculiar nature of a man, be compatible with good manners?
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is through his good manners that a man's peculiar nature should be made all the more conspicuous. Every one likes distinction, but it should not be disagreeable.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The most privileged position, in life as in society, is that of an educated soldier. Rough warriors, at any rate, remain true to their character, and as great strength is usually the cover for good nature, we get on with them at need.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: No one is more troublesome than an awkward civilian. As his business is not with anything brutal or coarse, he might be expected to show delicacy of feeling.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: When we live with people who have a delicate sense of what is fitting, we get quite anxious about them if anything happens to disturb this sense.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A familiar in the place of a respectful demeanour is always ridiculous.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There is no outward sign of politeness that will be found to lack some deep moral foundation. The right kind of education would be that which conveyed the sign and the foundation at the same time.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A man's manners are the mirror in which he shows his portrait.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There is a politeness of the heart, and it is allied to love. It produces the most agreeable politeness of outward demeanour.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Voluntary dependence is the best state, and how should that be possible without love?
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: We are never further from our wishes than when we fancy we possess the object of them.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: No one is more of a slave than he who thinks himself free without being so.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A man has only to declare himself free to feel at the same moment that he is limited. Should he venture to declare himself limited, he feels himself free.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Against the great superiority of another there is no remedy but love.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is a terrible thing for an eminent man to be gloried in by fools.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is said that no man is a hero to his valet. That is only because a hero can be recognised only by a hero. The valet will probably know how to appreciate his like,—his fellow-valet.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There is no greater consolation for mediocrity than that the genius is not immortal.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The greatest men are linked to their age by some weak point.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: We generally take men to be more dangerous than they are.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Fools and wise folk are alike harmless. It is the half-wise, and the half-foolish, who are the most dangerous.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: To see a difficult thing lightly handled gives us the impression of the impossible.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Difficulties increase the nearer we come to our aim.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Sowing is not so painful as reaping.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: We are fond of looking to the future, because our secret wishes make us apt to turn in our favour the uncertainties which move about in it hither and thither.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is not easy to be in any great assembly without thinking that the chance which brings so many people together will also make us meet our friends.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A man may live never so retired a life but he becomes a debtor or a creditor before he is aware of it.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: If anyone meets us who owes us a debt of gratitude, it immediately crosses our mind. How often can we meet some one to whom we owe gratitude, without thinking of it!
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: To communicate oneself is Nature; to receive a communication as it is given is Culture.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: No one would speak much in society if he were aware how often we misunderstand others.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is only because we have not understood a thing that we cannot repeat it without alteration.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: To make a long speech in the presence of others without flattering your audience, is to rouse dislike.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Every word that we utter rouses its contrary.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Contradiction and flattery make, both of them, bad conversation.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The pleasantest society is that in which there exists a genial deference amongst the members one towards another.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: By nothing do men show their character more than by the things they laugh at.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The ridiculous springs from a moral contrast innocently presented to the senses.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The sensual man often laughs when there is nothing to laugh at. Whatever it is that moves him, he shows that he is pleased with himself.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: An intelligent man finds almost everything ridiculous, a wise man hardly anything.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A man does not mind being blamed for his faults, and being punished for them, and he patiently suffers much for the sake of them; but he becomes impatient if he is required to give them up.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Certain faults are necessary to the individual if he is to exist. We should not like old friends to give up certain peculiarities.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is said of a man that he will soon die, when he acts in any way unlike himself.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: What kind of faults in ourselves should we retain, nay, even cultivate? Those which rather flatter other people than offend them.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The passions are good or bad qualities, only intensified.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Our passions are, in truth, like the phoenix. When the old one burns away, the new one rises out of its ashes at once.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Great passions are hopeless diseases. That which could cure them is the first thing to make them really dangerous.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Passion is enhanced and tempered by avowal. In nothing, perhaps, is the middle course more desirable than in confidence and reticence towards those we love.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: To sit in judgment on the departed is never likely to be equitable. We all suffer from life; who except God can call us to account? Let not their faults and sufferings, but what they have accomplished and done, occupy the survivors.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is failings that show human nature, and merits that distinguish the individual; faults and misfortunes we all have in common; virtues belong to each one separately.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The secret places in the way of life may not and cannot be revealed: there are rocks of offence on which every traveller must stumble. But the poet points to where they are.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It would not be worth while to see seventy years if all the wisdom of this world were foolishness with God.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The true is Godlike: we do not see it itself; we must guess at it through its manifestations.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The real scholar learns how to evolve the unknown from the known, and draws near the master.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: In the smithy the iron is softened by blowing up the fire, and taking the dross from the bar. As soon as it is purified, it is beaten and pressed, and becomes firm again by the addition of fresh water. The same thing happens to a man at the hands of his teacher.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: What belongs to a man, he cannot get rid of, even though he throws it away.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Of true religions there are only two: one of them recognises and worships the Holy that without form or shape dwells in and around us; and the other recognises and worships it in its fairest form. Everything that lies between these two is idolatry.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is undeniable that in the Reformation the human mind tried to free itself; and the renaissance of Greek and Roman antiquity brought about the wish and longing for a freer, more seemly, and elegant life. The movement was favoured in no small degree by the fact that men's hearts aimed at returning to a certain simple state of nature, while the imagination sought to concentrate itself.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: As a coal is revived by incense, so prayer revives the hopes of the heart.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: From a strict point of view we must have a reformation of ourselves every day, and protest against others, even though it be in no religious sense.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: As we grow older, the ordeals grow greater.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Where I cannot be moral, my power is gone.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A man is not deceived by others, he deceives himself.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is not the intelligent man who rules, but intelligence; not the wise man, but wisdom.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: To praise a man is to put oneself on his level.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is not enough to know, we must also apply; it is not enough to will, we must also do.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Chinese, Indian, and Egyptian antiquities are never more than curiosities; it is well to make acquaintance with them; but in point of moral and æsthetic culture they can help us little.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The German runs no greater danger than to advance with and by the example of his neighbours. There is perhaps no nation that is fitter for the process of self-development; so that it has proved of the greatest advantage to Germany to have obtained the notice of the world so late.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Even men of insight do not see that they try to explain things which lie at the foundation of our experience, and in which we must simply acquiesce. Yet still the attempt may have its advantage, as otherwise we should break off our researches too soon.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: From this time forward, if a man does not apply himself to some art or handiwork, he will be in a bad way. In the rapid changes of the world, knowledge is no longer a furtherance; by the time a man has taken note of everything, he has lost himself.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Besides, in these days the world forces universal culture upon us, and so we need not trouble ourselves further about it; we must appropriate some particular culture.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The greatest difficulties lie where we do not look for them.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Our interest in public events is mostly the merest philistinism.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Nothing is more highly to be prized than the value of each day.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Pereant qui ante nos nostra dixerunt! This is so strange an utterance, that it could only have come from one who fancied himself autochthonous. The man who looks upon it as an honour to be descended from wise ancestors, will allow them at least as much common-sense as he allows himself.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Strictly speaking, everything depends upon a man's intentions; where these exist, thoughts appear; and as the intentions are, so are the thoughts.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: If a man lives long in a high position, he does not, it is true, experience all that a man can experience; but he experiences things like them, and perhaps some things that have no parallel elsewhere.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The first and last thing that is required of genius is love of truth.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: To be and remain true to oneself and others, is to possess the noblest attribute of the greatest talents.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Great talents are the best means of conciliation.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The action of genius is in a way ubiquitous: towards general truths before experience, and towards particular truths after it.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: An active scepticism is one which constantly aims at overcoming itself, and arriving by means of regulated experience at a kind of conditioned certainty.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
idea: Scepticism can be a method for reaching provisional knowledge, rather than a permanent refusal to conclude. Experience disciplines doubt and also limits certainty.

text: The general nature of the sceptical mind is its tendency to inquire whether any particular predicate really attaches to any particular object; and the purpose of the inquiry is safely to apply in practice what has thus been discovered and proved.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The mind endowed with active powers and keeping with a practical object to the task that lies nearest, is the worthiest there is on earth.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Perfection is the measure of heaven, and the wish to be perfect the measure of man.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Not only what is born with him, but also what he acquires, makes the man.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A man is well equipped for all the real necessities of life if he trusts his senses, and so cultivates them that they remain worthy of being trusted.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The senses do not deceive; it is the judgment that deceives.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The lower animal is taught by its organs; man teaches his organs, and dominates them.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: When a great idea enters the world as a Gospel, it becomes an offence to the multitude, which stagnates in pedantry; and to those who have much learning but little depth, it is folly.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Every idea appears at first as a strange visitor, and when it begins to be realised, it is hardly distinguishable from phantasy and phantastery.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: This it is that has been called, in a good and in a bad sense, ideology; and this is why the ideologist is so repugnant to the hard-working, practical man of every day.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: You may recognise the utility of an idea, and yet not quite understand how to make a perfect use of it.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Credo Deum! That is a fine, a worthy thing to say; but to recognise God where and as he reveals himself, is the only true bliss on earth.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Kepler said: 'My wish is that I may perceive the God whom I find everywhere in the external world, in like manner also within and inside me.' The good man was not aware that in that very moment the divine in him stood in the closest connection with the divine in the Universe.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: What is predestination? It is this: God is mightier and wiser than we are, and so he does with us as he pleases.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Toleration should, strictly speaking, be only a passing mood; it ought to lead to acknowledgment and appreciation. To tolerate a person is to affront him.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Faith, Love, and Hope once felt, in a quiet sociable hour, a plastic impulse in their nature; they worked together and created a lovely image, a Pandora in the higher sense, Patience.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: 'I stumbled over the roots of the tree which I planted.' It must have been an old forester who said that.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A leaf blown by the wind often looks like a bird.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Does the sparrow know how the stork feels?
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Lamps make oil-spots, and candles want snuffing; it is only the light of heaven that shines pure and leaves no stain.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: If you miss the first button-hole, you will not succeed in buttoning up your coat.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A burnt child dreads the fire; an old man who has often been singed is afraid of warming himself.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is not worth while to do anything for the world that we have with us, as the existing order may in a moment pass away. It is for the past and the future that we must work: for the past, to acknowledge its merits; for the future, to try to increase its value.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Let every man ask himself with which of his faculties he can and will somehow influence his age.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Let no one think that people have waited for him as for the Saviour.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Character in matters great and small consists in a man steadily pursuing the things of which he feels himself capable.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The moment is a kind of public; a man must deceive it into believing that he is doing something; then it leaves us alone to go our way in secret; whereat its grandchildren cannot fail to be astonished.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There are men who put their knowledge in the place of insight.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There is no sadder sight than the direct striving after the unconditioned in this thoroughly conditioned world.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Before the Revolution it was all effort; afterwards it all changed to demand.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Can a nation become ripe? That is a strange question. I would answer, Yes! if all the men could be born thirty years of age. But as youth will always be too forward and old age too backward, the really mature man is always hemmed in between them, and has to resort to strange devices to make his way through.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Vanity is a desire of personal glory, the wish to be appreciated, honoured, and run after, not because of one's personal qualities, merits, and achievements, but because of one's individual existence. At best, therefore, it is a frivolous beauty whom it befits.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Both what is reasonable and what is unreasonable have to undergo the like contradiction.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Dialectic is the culture of the spirit of contradiction, which is given to man that he may learn to perceive the differences between things.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: With those who are really of like disposition with himself a man cannot long be at variance; he will always come to an agreement again. With those who are really of adverse disposition, he may in vain try to preserve harmony; he will always come to a separation again.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Opponents fancy they refute us when they repeat their own opinion and pay no attention to ours.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: People who contradict and dispute should now and then remember that not every mode of speech is intelligible to every one.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Every man hears only what he understands.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: I am quite prepared to find that many a reader will disagree with me; but when he has a thing before him in black and white, he must let it stand. Another reader may perhaps take up the very same copy and agree with me.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The truest liberality is appreciation.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: For the strenuous man the difficulty is to recognise the merits of elder contemporaries and not let himself be hindered by their defects.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Some men think about the defects of their friends, and there is nothing to be gained by it. I have always paid attention to the merits of my enemies, and found it an advantage.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There are many men who fancy they understand whatever they experience.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: When a man grows old he must consciously remain at a certain stage.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It does not become an old man to run after the fashion, either in thought or in dress. But he must know where he is, and what the others are aiming at. What is called fashion is the tradition of the moment. All tradition carries with it a certain necessity for people to put themselves on a level with it.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: We have long been busy with the critique of reason. I should like to see a critique of common-sense. It would be a real benefit to mankind if we could convincingly prove to the ordinary intelligence how far it can go; and that is just as much as it fully requires for life on this earth.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The thinker makes a great mistake when he asks after cause and effect: they both together make up the indivisible phenomenon.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: All practical men try to bring the world under their hands; all thinkers, under their heads. How far each succeeds, they may both see for themselves.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Shall we say that a man thinks only when he cannot think out that of which he is thinking?
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: What is invention or discovery? It is the conclusion of what we were looking for.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is with history as with nature and with everything of any depth, it may be past, present, or future: the further we seriously pursue it, the more difficult are the problems that appear. The man who is not afraid of them, but attacks them bravely, has a feeling of higher culture and greater ease the further he progresses.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Every phenomenon is within our reach if we treat it as an inclined plane, which is of easy ascent, though the thick end of the wedge may be steep and inaccessible.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: If a man would enter upon some course of knowledge, he must either be deceived or deceive himself, unless external necessity irresistibly determines him. Who would become a physician if, at one and the same time, he saw before him all the horrible sights that await him?
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: How many years must a man do nothing before he can at all know what is to be done and how to do it!
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Duty: where a man loves what he commands himself to do.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: When Madame Roland was on the scaffold, she asked for pen and paper, to note the peculiar thoughts that hovered about her on the last journey. It is a pity they were refused, for in a tranquil mind thoughts rise up at the close of life hitherto unthinkable; like blessed inward voices, alighting in glory on the summits of the past.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Literature is a fragment of fragments: the least of what happened and was spoken, has been written; and of the things that have been written, very few have been preserved.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Excellent work is unfathomable, approach it as you will.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The appeal to posterity springs from the pure, strong feeling of the existence of something imperishable; something that, even though it be not at once recognised, will in the end be gratified by finding the minority turn into a majority.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: When a new literature succeeds, it obscures the effect of an earlier one, and its own effect predominates; so that it is well, from time to time, to look back. What is original in us is best preserved and quickened if we do not lose sight of those who have gone before us.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The most original authors of modern times are so, not because they produce what is new, but only because they are able to say things the like of which seem never to have been said before.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There are many thoughts that come only from general culture, like buds from green branches. When roses bloom, you see them blooming everywhere.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Lucidity is a due distribution of light and shade.' Hamann.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A man who has no acquaintance with foreign languages knows nothing of his own.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: We must remember that there are many men who, without being productive, are anxious to say something important, and the results are most curious.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Deep and earnest thinkers are in a difficult position with regard to the public.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Some books seem to have been written, not to teach us anything, but to let us know that the author has known something.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: An author can show no greater respect for his public than by never bringing it what it expects, but what he himself thinks right and proper in that stage of his own and others' culture in which for the time he finds himself.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The so-called Nature-poets are men of active talent, with a fresh stimulus and reaction from an over-cultured, stagnant, mannered epoch of art. They cannot avoid commonplace.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Productions are now possible which, without being bad, have no value. They have no value, because they contain nothing; and they are not bad, because a general form of good-workmanship is present to the author's mind.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: All lyrical work must, as a whole, be perfectly intelligible, but in some particulars a little unintelligible.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A romance is a subjective epic in which the author begs leave to treat the world after his own ideas. The only question is, whether he has any ideas; the rest will follow of itself.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Superstition is the poetry of life, and so it does not hurt the poet to be superstitious.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: That glorious hymn, Veni Creator Spiritus, is really an appeal to genius. That is why it speaks so powerfully to men of intellect and power.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Translators are like busy match-makers: they sing the praises of some half-veiled beauty, and extol her charms, and arouse an irresistible longing for the original.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A Spinoza in poetry becomes a Machiavelli in philosophy.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Against the three unities there is nothing to be said, if the subject is very simple; but there are times when thrice three unities, skilfully interwoven, produce a very pleasant effect.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The sentimentality of the English is humorous and tender; of the French, popular and pathetic; of the Germans, naïve and realistic.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Mysticism is the scholastic of the heart, the dialectic of the feelings.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: If a man sets out to reproach an author with obscurity, he should first of all examine his own mind, to see if he is himself all clearness within. Twilight makes even plain writing illegible.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: In psychological reflection the greatest difficulty is this: that inner and outer must always be viewed in parallel lines, or, rather, interwoven. It is a continual systole and diastole, an inspiration and an expiration of the living soul. If this cannot be put into words, it should be carefully marked and noted.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: My relations with Schiller rested on the decided tendency of both of us towards a single aim, and our common activity rested on the diversity of the means by which we endeavoured to attain that aim.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There may be eclectic philosophers, but not an eclectic philosophy.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Various maxims of the ancients, which we are wont to repeat again and again, had a meaning quite different from that which is apt to attach to them in later times.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The saying that no one who is unacquainted with or a stranger to geometry should enter the philosopher's school, does not mean that a man must become a mathematician to attain the wisdom of the world.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Geometry is here taken in its primary elements, such as are contained in Euclid and laid before every beginner; and then it is the most perfect propædeutic and introduction to philosophy.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Let us remember how great the ancients were; and especially how the Socratic school holds up to us the source and standard of all life and action, and bids us not indulge in empty speculation, but live and do.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: So long as our scholastic education takes us back to antiquity and furthers the study of the Greek and Latin languages, we may congratulate ourselves that these studies, so necessary for the higher culture, will never disappear.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: If we set our gaze on antiquity and earnestly study it, in the desire to form ourselves thereon, we get the feeling as if it were only then that we really became men.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The pedagogue, in trying to write and speak Latin, has a higher and grander idea of himself than would be permissible in ordinary life.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: In the presence of antiquity, the mind that is susceptible to poetry and art feels itself placed in the most pleasing ideal state of nature; and even to this day the Homeric hymns have the power of freeing us, at any rate, for moments, from the frightful burden which the tradition of several thousand years has rolled upon us.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There is no such thing as patriotic art and patriotic science. Both art and science belong, like all things great and good, to the whole world, and can be furthered only by a free and general interchange of ideas among contemporaries, with continual reference to the heritage of the past as it is known to us.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Poetical talent is given to peasant as well as to knight; all that is required is that each shall grasp his position and treat it worthily.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: An historic sense means a sense so cultured that, in valuing the deserts and merits of its own time, it takes account also of the past.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The best that history gives us is the enthusiasm it arouses.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The historian's duty is to separate the true from the false, the certain from the uncertain, and the doubtful from that which cannot be accepted.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is seldom that any one of great age becomes historical to himself, and finds his contemporaries become historical to him, so that he neither cares nor is able to argue with any one.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: We really learn only from those books which we cannot criticise. The author of a book which we could criticise would have to learn from us.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: That is the reason why the Bible will never lose its power; because, as long as the world lasts, no one can stand up and say: I grasp it as a whole and understand all the parts of it. But we say humbly: as a whole it is worthy of respect, and in all its parts it is applicable.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There is and will be much discussion as to the use and harm of circulating the Bible. One thing is clear to me: mischief will result, as heretofore, by using it phantastically as a system of dogma; benefit, as heretofore, by a loving acceptance of its teachings.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: I am convinced that the Bible will always be more beautiful the more it is understood; the more, that is, we see and observe that every word which we take in a general sense and apply specially to ourselves, had, under certain circumstances of time and place, a peculiar, special, and directly individual reference.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The incurable evil of religious controversy is that while one party wants to connect the highest interest of humanity with fables and phrases, the other tries to rest it on things that satisfy no one.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: If one has not read the newspapers for some months and then reads them all together, one sees, as one never saw before, how much time is wasted with this kind of literature.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The classical is health; and the romantic, disease.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Ovid remained classical even in exile: it is not in himself that he sees misfortune, but in his banishment from the metropolis of the world.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The romantic is already fallen into its own abysm. It is hard to imagine anything more degraded than the worst of the new productions.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Bodies which rot while they are still alive, and are edified by the detailed contemplation of their own decay; dead men who remain in the world for the ruin of others, and feed their death on the living,—to this have come our makers of literature. When the same thing happened in antiquity, it was only as a strange token of some rare disease; but with the moderns the disease has become endemic and epidemic.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Literature decays only as men become more and more corrupt.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: What a day it is when we must envy the men in their graves!
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The things that are true, good, excellent, are simple and always alike, whatever their appearance may be. But the error that we blame is extremely manifold and varying; it is in conflict not only with the good and the true, but also with itself; it is self-contradictory. Thus it is that the words of blame in our literature must necessarily outnumber the words of praise.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The Greeks, whose poetry and rhetoric was of a simple and positive character, express approval more often than disapproval. With the Latin writers it is the contrary; and the more poetry and the arts of speech decay, the more will blame swell and praise shrink.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There are certain empirical enthusiasts who are quite right in showing their enthusiasm over new productions that are good; but they are as ecstatic as if there were no other good work in the world at all.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: In Sakontala the poet appears in his highest function. As the representative of the most natural condition of things, the finest mode of life, the purest moral endeavour, the worthiest majesty, and the most solemn worship, he ventures on common and ridiculous contrasts.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Shakespeare's Henry IV. If everything were lost that has ever been preserved to us of this kind of writing, the arts of poetry and rhetoric could be completely restored out of this one play.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Shakespeare's finest dramas are wanting here and there in facility: they are something more than they should be, and for that very reason indicate the great poet.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Shakespeare is dangerous reading for budding talents: he compels them to reproduce him, and they fancy they are producing themselves.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Yorick Sterne was the finest spirit that ever worked. To read him is to attain a fine feeling of freedom; his humour is inimitable, and it is not every kind of humour that frees the soul.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The peculiar value of so-called popular ballads is that their motives are drawn direct from nature. This, however, is an advantage of which the poet of culture could also avail himself, if he knew how to do it.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: When we say of a landscape that it has a romantic character, it is the secret feeling of the sublime taking the form of the past, or, what is the same thing, of solitude, absence, or seclusion.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The Beautiful is a manifestation of secret laws of nature, which, without its presence, would never have been revealed.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is said: Artist, study nature! But it is no trifle to develop the noble out of the commonplace, or beauty out of uniformity.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: When Nature begins to reveal her open secret to a man, he feels an irresistible longing for her worthiest interpreter, Art.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: For all other Arts we must make some allowance; but to Greek Art alone we are always debtors.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There is no surer way of evading the world than by Art; and no surer way of uniting with it than by Art.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Even in the moments of highest happiness and deepest misery we need the Artist.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: False tendencies of the senses are a kind of desire after realism, always better than that false tendency which expresses itself as idealistic longing.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The dignity of Art appears perhaps most conspicuously in Music; for in Music there is no material to be deducted. It is wholly form and intrinsic value, and it raises and ennobles all that it expresses.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is only by Art, and especially by Poetry, that the imagination is regulated. Nothing is more frightful than imagination without taste.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: If we were to despise Art on the ground that it is an imitation of Nature, it might be answered that Nature also imitates much else; further, that Art does not exactly imitate that which can be seen by the eyes, but goes back to that element of reason of which Nature consists and according to which Nature acts.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Further, the Arts also produce much out of themselves, and, on the other hand, add much where Nature fails in perfection, in that they possess beauty in themselves. So it was that Pheidias could sculpture a god although he had nothing that could be seen by the eye to imitate, but grasped the appearance which Zeus himself would have if he were to come before our eyes.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Art rests upon a kind of religious sense: it is deeply and ineradicably in earnest. Thus it is that Art so willingly goes hand in hand with Religion.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A noble philosopher spoke of architecture as frozen music; and it was inevitable that many people should shake their heads over his remark. We believe that no better repetition of this fine thought can be given than by calling architecture a speechless music.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Art is essentially noble; therefore the artist has nothing to fear from a low or common subject. Nay, by taking it up, he ennobles it; and so it is that we see the greatest artists boldly exercising their sovereign rights.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: In every artist there is a germ of daring, without which no talent is conceivable.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: All the artists who are already known to me from so many sides, I propose to consider exclusively from the ethical side; to explain from the subject-matter and method of their work the part played therein by time and place, nation and master, and their own indestructible personality; to mould them to what they became and to preserve them in what they were.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Art is a medium of what no tongue can utter; and thus it seems a piece of folly to try to convey its meaning afresh by means of words. But, by trying to do so, the understanding gains; and this, again, benefits the faculty in practice.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: An artist who produces valuable work is not always able to give an account of his own or others' performances.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: We know of no world except in relation to mankind; and we wish for no Art that does not bear the mark of this relation.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Higher aims are in themselves more valuable, even if unfulfilled, than lower ones quite attained.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Blunt naïvety, stubborn vigour, scrupulous observance of rule, and any other epithets which may apply to older German Art, are a part of every earlier and simpler artistic method. The older Venetians, Florentines, and others had it all too.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Because Albrecht Dürer, with his incomparable talent, could never rise to the idea of the symmetry of beauty, or even to the thought of a fitting conformity to the object in view, are we never to spurn the ground!
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Albrecht Dürer had the advantage of a very profound realistic perception, an affectionate human sympathy with all present conditions. He was kept back by a gloomy phantasy, devoid both of form and foundation.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It would be interesting to show how Martin Schön stands near him, and how the merits of German Art were restricted to these two; and useful also to show that it was not evening every day.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: In every Italian school the butterfly breaks loose from the chrysalis.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: After Klopstock released us from rhyme, and Voss gave us models of prose, are we to make doggerel again like Hans Sachs?
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Let us be many-sided! Turnips are good, but they are best mixed with chestnuts. And these two noble products of the earth grow far apart.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: In every kind of Art there is a degree of excellence which may be reached, so to speak, by the mere use of one's own natural talents. But at the same time it is impossible to go beyond that point, unless Art comes to one's aid.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: In the presence of Nature even moderate talent is always possessed of insight; hence drawings from Nature that are at all carefully done always give pleasure.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: To make many sketches issue at last in a complete work is something that not even the best artists always achieve.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: In the sphere of true Art there is no preparatory school, but there is a way of preparation; and the best preparation is the interest of the most insignificant pupil in the work of the master. Colour-grinders have often made excellent painters.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: If an artist grasps Nature aright and contrives to give its form a nobler, freer grace, no one will understand the source of his inspiration, and every one will swear that he has taken it from the antique.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: In studying the human form, let the painter reject what is exaggerated, false, and mechanical; but let him learn to grasp of what infinite grace the human body is capable.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Kant taught us the critique of the reason. We must have a critique of the senses if Art in general, and especially German Art, is ever to regain its tone and move forward on the path of life and happiness.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: In the sphere of natural science let us remember that we have always to deal with an insoluble problem. Let us prove keen and honest in attending to anything which is in any way brought to our notice, most of all when it does not fit in with our previous ideas. For it is only thereby that we perceive the problem, which does indeed lie in nature, but still more in man.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A man cannot well stand by himself, and so he is glad to join a party; because if he does not find rest there, he at any rate finds quiet and safety.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is a misfortune to pass at once from observation to conclusion, and to regard both as of equal value; but it befalls many a student.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: First let a man teach himself, and then he will be taught by others.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Theories are usually the over-hasty efforts of an impatient understanding that would gladly be rid of phenomena, and so puts in their place pictures, notions, nay, often mere words. We may surmise, or even see quite well, that such theories are make-shifts; but do not passion and party-spirit love a make-shift at all times? And rightly, too, because they stand in so much need of it.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is difficult to know how to treat the errors of the age. If a man oppose them, he stands alone; if he surrender to them, they bring him neither joy nor credit.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There are some hundred Christian sects, every one of them acknowledging God and the Lord in its own way, without troubling themselves further about one another. In the study of nature, nay, in every study, things must of necessity come to the same pass. For what is the meaning of every one speaking of toleration, and trying to prevent others from thinking and expressing themselves after their own fashion?
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: To communicate knowledge by means of analogy appears to me a process equally useful and pleasant. The analogous case is not there to force itself on the attention or prove anything; it offers a comparison with some other case, but is not in union with it. Several analogous cases do not join to form a seried row: they are like good society, which always suggests more than it grants.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: To err is to be as though truth did not exist. To lay bare the error to oneself and others is retrospective discovery.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: With the growth of knowledge our ideas must from time to time be organised afresh. The change takes place usually in accordance with new maxims as they arise, but it always remains provisional.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: When we find facts within our knowledge exhibited by some new method, or even, it may be, described in a foreign language, they receive a peculiar charm of novelty and wear a fresh air.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: If two masters of the same art differ in their statement of it, in all likelihood the insoluble problem lies midway between them.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The orbits of certainties touch one another; but in the interstices there is room enough for error to go forth and prevail.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: We more readily confess to errors, mistakes, and shortcomings in our conduct than in our thought.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: This also explains how it is that truths which have been recognised are at first tacitly admitted, and then gradually spread, so that the very thing which was obstinately denied appears at last as something quite natural.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Ignorant people raise questions which were answered by the wise thousands of years ago.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: When a man sees a phenomenon before him, his thoughts often range beyond it; when he hears it only talked about, he has no thoughts at all.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Authority. Man cannot exist without it, and yet it brings in its train just as much of error as of truth. It perpetuates one by one things which should pass away one by one; it rejects that which should be preserved and allows it to pass away; and it is chiefly to blame for mankind's want of progress.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Authority—the fact, namely, that something has already happened or been said or decided, is of great value; but it is only a pedant who demands authority for everything.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: An old foundation is worthy of all respect, but it must not take from us the right to build afresh wherever we will.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Our advice is that every man should remain in the path he has struck out for himself, and refuse to be overawed by authority, hampered by prevalent opinion, or carried away by fashion.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The various branches of knowledge always tend as a whole to stray away from life, and return thither only by a roundabout way.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: For they are, in truth, text-books of life: they gather outer and inner experiences into a general and connected whole.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: An important fact, an ingenious aperçu, occupies a very great number of men, at first only to make acquaintance with it; then to understand it; and afterwards to work it out and carry it further.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: On the appearance of anything new the mass of people ask: What is the use of it? And they are not wrong. For it is only through the use of anything that they can perceive its value.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The truly wise ask what the thing is in itself and in relation to other things, and do not trouble themselves about the use of it,—in other words, about the way in which it may be applied to the necessities of existence and what is already known. This will soon be discovered by minds of a very different order—minds that feel the joy of living, and are keen, adroit, and practical.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Every investigator must before all things look upon himself as one who is summoned to serve on a jury. He has only to consider how far the statement of the case is complete and clearly set forth by the evidence. Then he draws his conclusion and gives his vote, whether it be that his opinion coincides with that of the foreman or not.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: In the world of science, however, these sentiments have never been of much account. There everything depends on making opinion prevail and dominate; few men are really independent; the majority draws the individual after it.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The history of philosophy, of science, of religion, all shows that opinions spread in masses, but that that always comes to the front which is more easily grasped, that is to say, is most suited and agreeable to the human mind in its ordinary condition. Nay, he who has practised self-culture in the higher sense may always reckon upon meeting an adverse majority.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There is much that is true which does not admit of being calculated; just as there are a great many things that cannot be brought to the test of a decisive experiment.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is just for this that man stands so high, that what could not otherwise be brought to light should be brought to light in him. What is a musical string, and all its mechanical division, in comparison with the musician's ear? May we not also say, what are the elementary phenomena of nature itself compared with man, who must control and modify them all before he can in any way assimilate them to himself?
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: To a new truth there is nothing more hurtful than an old error.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The ultimate origin of things is completely beyond our faculties; hence when we see anything come into being, we look upon it as having been already there. This is why we find the theory of emboîtement intelligible.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There are many problems in natural science on which we cannot fittingly speak unless we call metaphysics to our aid; but not the wisdom of the schools, which consists in mere verbiage. It is that which was before physics, exists with it, and will be after it.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A man must cling to the belief that the incomprehensible is comprehensible; otherwise he would not try to fathom it.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There are pedants who are also rascals, and they are the worst of all.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A man does not need to have seen or experienced everything himself. But if he is to commit himself to another's experiences and his way of putting them, let him consider that he has to do with three things—the object in question and two subjects.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The supreme achievement would be to see that stating a fact is starting a theory.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: If I acquiesce at last in some ultimate fact of nature, it is, no doubt, only resignation; but it makes a great difference whether the resignation takes place at the limits of human faculty, or within the hypothetical boundaries of my own narrow individuality.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: If we look at the problems raised by Aristotle, we are astonished at his gift of observation. What wonderful eyes the Greeks had for many things! Only they committed the mistake of being over-hasty, of passing straightway from the phenomenon to the explanation of it, and thereby produced certain theories that are quite inadequate. But this is the mistake of all times, and still made in our own day.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Hypotheses are cradle-songs by which the teacher lulls his scholars to sleep. The thoughtful and honest observer is always learning more and more of his limitations; he sees that the further knowledge spreads, the more numerous are the problems that make their appearance.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Our mistake is that we doubt what is certain and want to establish what is uncertain. My maxim in the study of Nature is this: hold fast what is certain and keep a watch on what is uncertain.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: What a master a man would be in his own subject if he taught nothing useless!
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The greatest piece of folly is that every man thinks himself compelled to hand down what people think they have known.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: If many a man did not feel obliged to repeat what is untrue, because he has said it once, the world would have been quite different.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There is nothing more odious than the majority; it consists of a few powerful men to lead the way; of accommodating rascals and submissive weaklings; and of a mass of men who trot after them, without in the least knowing their own mind.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: We praise the eighteenth century for concerning itself chiefly with analysis. The task remaining to the nineteenth is to discover the false syntheses which prevail, and to analyse their contents anew.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A school may be regarded as a single individual who talks to himself for a hundred years, and takes an extraordinary pleasure in his own being, however foolish and silly it may be.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: In science it is a service of the highest merit to seek out those fragmentary truths attained by the ancients, and to develop them further.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: If a man devotes himself to the promotion of science, he is firstly opposed, and then he is informed that his ground is already occupied. At first men will allow no value to what we tell them, and then they behave as if they knew it all themselves.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Nature fills all space with her limitless productivity. If we observe merely our own earth, everything that we call evil and unfortunate is so because Nature cannot provide room for everything that comes into existence, and still less endow it with permanence.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Everything that comes into being seeks room for itself and desires duration: hence it drives something else from its place and shortens its duration.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There is so much of cryptogamy in phanerogamy that centuries will not decipher it.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: What a true saying it is that he who wants to deceive mankind must before all things make absurdity plausible.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The further knowledge advances, the nearer we come to the unfathomable: the more we know how to use our knowledge, the better we see that the unfathomable is of no practical use.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The finest achievement for a man of thought is to have fathomed what may be fathomed, and quietly to revere the unfathomable.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The discerning man who acknowledges his limitations is not far off perfection.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: There are two things of which a man cannot be careful enough: of obstinacy if he confines himself to his own line of thought; of incompetency, if he goes beyond it.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Incompetency is a greater obstacle to perfection than one would think.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The century advances; but every individual begins anew.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: What friends do with us and for us is a real part of our life; for it strengthens and advances our personality. The assault of our enemies is not part of our life; it is only part of our experience; we throw it off and guard ourselves against it as against frost, storm, rain, hail, or any other of the external evils which may be expected to happen.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: A man cannot live with every one, and therefore he cannot live for every one. To see this truth aright is to place a high value upon one's friends, and not to hate or persecute one's enemies. Nay, there is hardly any greater advantage for a man to gain than to find out, if he can, the merits of his opponents: it gives him a decided ascendency over them.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: Every one knows how to value what he has attained in life; most of all the man who thinks and reflects in his old age. He has a comfortable feeling that it is something of which no one can rob him.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: The best metempsychosis is for us to appear again in others.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: It is very seldom that we satisfy ourselves; all the more consoling is it to have satisfied others.
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe

text: We look back upon our life only as on a thing of broken pieces, because our misses and failures are always the first to strike us, and outweigh in our imagination what we have done, and attained.

author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Whatever great advantages nature may give, it is not she alone, but fortune also that makes the hero.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The contempt of riches in philosophers was only a hidden desire to avenge their merit upon the injustice of fortune, by despising the very goods of which fortune had deprived them; it was a secret to guard themselves against the degradation of poverty, it was a back way by which to arrive at that distinction which they could not gain by riches.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The hate of favourites is only a love of favour. The envy of NOT possessing it, consoles and softens its regrets by the contempt it evinces for those who possess it, and we refuse them our homage, not being able to detract from them what attracts that of the rest of the world.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: To establish ourselves in the world we do everything to appear as if we were established.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Although men flatter themselves with their great actions, they are not so often the result of a great design as of chance.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It would seem that our actions have lucky or unlucky stars to which they owe a great part of the blame or praise which is given them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are no accidents so unfortunate from which skilful men will not draw some advantage, nor so fortunate that foolish men will not turn them to their hurt.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Fortune turns all things to the advantage of those on whom she smiles.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The happiness or unhappiness of men depends no less upon their dispositions than their fortunes.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Sincerity is an openness of heart; we find it in very few people; what we usually see is only an artful dissimulation to win the confidence of others.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The aversion to lying is often a hidden ambition to render our words credible and weighty, and to attach a religious aspect to our conversation.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Truth does not do as much good in the world, as its counterfeits do evil.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There is no praise we have not lavished upon Prudence; and yet she cannot assure to us the most trifling event.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: A clever man ought to so regulate his interests that each will fall in due order. Our greediness so often troubles us, making us run after so many things at the same time, that while we too eagerly look after the least we miss the greatest.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: What grace is to the body good sense is to the mind.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: If there is a pure love, exempt from the mixture of our other passions, it is that which is concealed at the bottom of the heart and of which even ourselves are ignorant.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There is no disguise which can long hide love where it exists, nor feign it where it does not.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are few people who would not be ashamed of being beloved when they love no longer.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: If we judge of love by the majority of its results it rather resembles hatred than friendship.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There is only one sort of love, but there are a thousand different copies.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Neither love nor fire can subsist without perpetual motion; both cease to live so soon as they cease to hope, or to fear.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There is real love just as there are real ghosts; every person speaks of it, few persons have seen it.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Love lends its name to an infinite number of engagements (Commerces) which are attributed to it, but with which it has no more concern than the Doge has with all that is done in Venice.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The love of justice is simply in the majority of men the fear of suffering injustice.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Silence is the best resolve for him who distrusts himself.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: What renders us so changeable in our friendship is, that it is difficult to know the qualities of the soul, but easy to know those of the mind.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We can love nothing but what agrees with us, and we can only follow our taste or our pleasure when we prefer our friends to ourselves; nevertheless it is only by that preference that friendship can be true and perfect.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Reconciliation with our enemies is but a desire to better our condition, a weariness of war, the fear of some unlucky accident.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: What men term friendship is merely a partnership with a collection of reciprocal interests, and an exchange of favours—in fact it is but a trade in which self love always expects to gain something.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is more disgraceful to distrust than to be deceived by our friends.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We often persuade ourselves to love people who are more powerful than we are, yet interest alone produces our friendship; we do not give our hearts away for the good we wish to do, but for that we expect to receive.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Our distrust of another justifies his deceit.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Men would not live long in society were they not the dupes of each other.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Self love increases or diminishes for us the good qualities of our friends, in proportion to the satisfaction we feel with them, and we judge of their merit by the manner in which they act towards us.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Everyone blames his memory, no one blames his judgment.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: In the intercourse of life, we please more by our faults than by our good qualities.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The largest ambition has the least appearance of ambition when it meets with an absolute impossibility in compassing its object.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: To awaken a man who is deceived as to his own merit is to do him as bad a turn as that done to the Athenian madman who was happy in believing that all the ships touching at the port belonged to him.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Old men delight in giving good advice as a consolation for the fact that they can no longer set bad examples.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Great names degrade instead of elevating those who know not how to sustain them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The test of extraordinary merit is to see those who envy it the most yet obliged to praise it.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: A man is perhaps ungrateful, but often less chargeable with ingratitude than his benefactor is.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We are deceived if we think that mind and judgment are two different matters: judgment is but the extent of the light of the mind. This light penetrates to the bottom of matters; it remarks all that can be remarked, and perceives what appears imperceptible. Therefore we must agree that it is the extent of the light in the mind that produces all the effects which we attribute to judgment.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Everyone praises his heart, none dare praise their understanding.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)
