text: Politeness of mind consists in thinking chaste and refined thoughts.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Gallantry of mind is saying the most empty things in an agreeable manner.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Ideas often flash across our minds more complete than we could make them after much labour.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The head is ever the dupe of the heart.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Those who know their minds do not necessarily know their hearts.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Men and things have each their proper perspective; to judge rightly of some it is necessary to see them near, of others we can never judge rightly but at a distance.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: A man for whom accident discovers sense, is not a rational being. A man only is so who understands, who distinguishes, who tests it.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: To understand matters rightly we should understand their details, and as that knowledge is almost infinite, our knowledge is always superficial and imperfect.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: One kind of flirtation is to boast we never flirt.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The head cannot long play the part of the heart.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Youth changes its tastes by the warmth of its blood, age retains its tastes by habit.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Nothing is given so profusely as advice.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The blemishes of the mind, like those of the face, increase by age.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There may be good but there are no pleasant marriages.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We are inconsolable at being deceived by our enemies and betrayed by our friends, yet still we are often content to be thus served by ourselves.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is as easy unwittingly to deceive oneself as to deceive others.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Nothing is less sincere than the way of asking and giving advice. The person asking seems to pay deference to the opinion of his friend, while thinking in reality of making his friend approve his opinion and be responsible for his conduct. The person giving the advice returns the confidence placed in him by eager and disinterested zeal, in doing which he is usually guided only by his own interest or reputation.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The most subtle of our acts is to simulate blindness for snares that we know are set for us. We are never so easily deceived as when trying to deceive.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The intention of never deceiving often exposes us to deception.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We often act treacherously more from weakness than from a fixed motive.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We frequently do good to enable us with impunity to do evil.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: If we conquer our passions it is more from their weakness than from our strength.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: If we never flattered ourselves we should have but scant pleasure.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The most deceitful persons spend their lives in blaming deceit, so as to use it on some great occasion to promote some great interest.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The daily employment of cunning marks a little mind, it generally happens that those who resort to it in one respect to protect themselves lay themselves open to attack in another.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Cunning and treachery are the offspring of incapacity.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The true way to be deceived is to think oneself more knowing than others.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Too great cleverness is but deceptive delicacy, true delicacy is the most substantial cleverness.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is sometimes necessary to play the fool to avoid being deceived by cunning men.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Weakness is the only fault which cannot be cured.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is far easier to be wise for others than to be so for oneself.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The only good examples are those, that make us see the absurdity of bad originals.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We are never so ridiculous from the habits we have as from those that we affect to have.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We sometimes differ more widely from ourselves than we do from others.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are some who never would have loved if they never had heard it spoken of.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: When not prompted by vanity we say little.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: A man would rather say evil of himself than say nothing.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: If it was not for the company of fools, a witty man would often be greatly at a loss.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We often boast that we are never bored, but yet we are so conceited that we do not perceive how often we bore others.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: As it is the mark of great minds to say many things in a few words, so it is that of little minds to use many words to say nothing.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is oftener by the estimation of our own feelings that we exaggerate the good qualities of others than by their merit, and when we praise them we wish to attract their praise.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We do not like to praise, and we never praise without a motive. Praise is flattery, artful, hidden, delicate, which gratifies differently him who praises and him who is praised. The one takes it as the reward of merit, the other bestows it to show his impartiality and knowledge.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We often select envenomed praise which, by a reaction upon those we praise, shows faults we could not have shown by other means.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Usually we only praise to be praised.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Few are sufficiently wise to prefer censure which is useful to praise which is treacherous.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Some reproaches praise; some praises reproach.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The refusal of praise is only the wish to be praised twice.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The desire which urges us to deserve praise strengthens our good qualities, and praise given to wit, valour, and beauty, tends to increase them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is easier to govern others than to prevent being governed.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: If we never flattered ourselves the flattery of others would not hurt us.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Nature makes merit but fortune sets it to work.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Fortune cures us of many faults that reason could not.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are some persons who only disgust with their abilities, there are persons who please even with their faults.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are persons whose only merit consists in saying and doing stupid things at the right time, and who ruin all if they change their manners.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The fame of great men ought always to be estimated by the means used to acquire it.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Flattery is base coin to which only our vanity gives currency.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is not enough to have great qualities, we should also have the management of them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: However brilliant an action it should not be esteemed great unless the result of a great motive.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: A certain harmony should be kept between actions and ideas if we desire to estimate the effects that they produce.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The art of using moderate abilities to advantage wins praise, and often acquires more reputation than real brilliancy.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Numberless arts appear foolish whose secre{t} motives are most wise and weighty.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is much easier to seem fitted for posts we do not fill than for those we do.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Ability wins us the esteem of the true men, luck that of the people.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The world oftener rewards the appearance of merit than merit itself.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Avarice is more opposed to economy than to liberality.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: However deceitful hope may be, yet she carries us on pleasantly to the end of life.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Idleness and fear keeps us in the path of duty, but our virtue often gets the praise.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: If one acts rightly and honestly, it is difficult to decide whether it is the effect of integrity or skill.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: As rivers are lost in the sea so are virtues in self.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: If we thoroughly consider the varied effects of indifference we find we miscarry more in our duties than in our interests.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are different kinds of curiosity: one springs from interest, which makes us desire to know everything that may be profitable to us; another from pride, which springs from a desire of knowing what others are ignorant of.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is far better to accustom our mind to bear the ills we have than to speculate on those which may befall us.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Constancy in love is a perpetual inconstancy which causes our heart to attach itself to all the qualities of the person we love in succession, sometimes giving the preference to one, sometimes to another. This constancy is merely inconstancy fixed, and limited to the same person.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are two kinds of constancy in love, one arising from incessantly finding in the loved one fresh objects to love, the other from regarding it as a point of honour to be constant.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Perseverance is not deserving of blame or praise, as it is merely the continuance of tastes and feelings which we can neither create or destroy.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: What makes us like new studies is not so much the weariness we have of the old or the wish for change as the desire to be admired by those who know more than ourselves, and the hope of advantage over those who know less.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We sometimes complain of the levity of our friends to justify our own by anticipation.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Our repentance is not so much sorrow for the ill we have done as fear of the ill that may happen to us.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: One sort of inconstancy springs from levity or weakness of mind, and makes us accept everyone's opinion, and another more excusable comes from a surfeit of matter.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Vices enter into the composition of virtues as poison into that of medicines. Prudence collects and blends the two and renders them useful against the ills of life.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: For the credit of virtue we must admit that the greatest misfortunes of men are those into which they fall through their crimes.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We admit our faults to repair by our sincerity the evil we have done in the opinion of others.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are both heroes of evil and heroes of good.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We do not despise all who have vices, but we do despise all who have not virtues.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The name of virtue is as useful to our interest as that of vice.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The health of the mind is not less uncertain than that of the body, and when passions seem furthest removed we are no less in danger of infection than of falling ill when we are well.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It seems that nature has at man's birth fixed the bounds of his virtues and vices.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Great men should not have great faults.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We may say vices wait on us in the course of our life as the landlords with whom we successively lodge, and if we travelled the road twice over I doubt if our experience would make us avoid them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: When our vices leave us we flatter ourselves with the idea we have left them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are relapses in the diseases of the mind as in those of the body; what we call a cure is often no more than an intermission or change of disease.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The defects of the mind are like the wounds of the body. Whatever care we take to heal them the scars ever remain, and there is always danger of their reopening.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The reason which often prevents us abandoning a single vice is having so many.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We easily forget those faults which are known only to ourselves.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are men of whom we can never believe evil without having seen it. Yet there are very few in whom we should be surprised to see it.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We exaggerate the glory of some men to detract from that of others, and we should praise Prince Conde and Marshal Turenne much less if we did not want to blame them both.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The desire to appear clever often prevents our being so.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Virtue would not go far did not vanity escort her.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: He who thinks he has the power to content the world greatly deceives himself, but he who thinks that the world cannot be content with him deceives himself yet more.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Falsely honest men are those who disguise their faults both to themselves and others; truly honest men are those who know them perfectly and confess them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: He is really wise who is nettled at nothing.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: He is a truly good man who desires always to bear the inspection of good men.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Folly follows us at all stages of life. If one appears wise 'tis but because his folly is proportioned to his age and fortune.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are foolish people who know and who skilfully use their folly.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Who lives without folly is not so wise as he thinks.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: In growing old we become more foolish—and more wise.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are people who are like farces, which are praised but for a time (however foolish and distasteful they may be).
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Most people judge men only by success or by fortune.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Love of glory, fear of shame, greed of fortune, the desire to make life agreeable and comfortable, and the wish to depreciate others are often causes of that bravery so vaunted among men.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Valour in common soldiers is a perilous method of earning their living.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Perfect valour is to do without witnesses what one would do before all the world.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Intrepidity is an extraordinary strength of soul which raises it above the troubles, disorders, and emotions which the sight of great perils can arouse in it: by this strength heroes maintain a calm aspect and preserve their reason and liberty in the most surprising and terrible accidents.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Hypocrisy is the homage vice pays to virtue.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Most men expose themselves in battle enough to save their honor, few wish to do so more than sufficiently, or than is necessary to make the design for which they expose themselves succeed.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We do not wish to lose life; we do wish to gain glory, and this makes brave men show more tact and address in avoiding death, than rogues show in preserving their fortunes.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Few persons on the first approach of age do not show wherein their body, or their mind, is beginning to fail.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Gratitude is as the good faith of merchants: it holds commerce together; and we do not pay because it is just to pay debts, but because we shall thereby more easily find people who will lend.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: All those who pay the debts of gratitude cannot thereby flatter themselves that they are grateful.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: What makes false reckoning, as regards gratitude, is that the pride of the giver and the receiver cannot agree as to the value of the benefit.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Too great a hurry to discharge of an obligation is a kind of ingratitude.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Lucky people are bad hands at correcting their faults; they always believe that they are right when fortune backs up their vice or folly.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Pride will not owe, self-love will not pay.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The good we have received from a man should make us excuse the wrong he does us.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Nothing is so infectious as example, and we never do great good or evil without producing the like. We imitate good actions by emulation, and bad ones by the evil of our nature, which shame imprisons until example liberates.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is great folly to wish only to be wise.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Whatever pretext we give to our afflictions it is always interest or vanity that causes them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is more often from pride than from ignorance that we are so obstinately opposed to current opinions; we find the first places taken, and we do not want to be the last.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We are easily consoled at the misfortunes of our friends when they enable us to prove our tenderness for them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It would seem that even self-love may be the dupe of goodness and forget itself when we work for others. And yet it is but taking the shortest way to arrive at its aim, taking usury under the pretext of giving, in fact winning everybody in a subtle and delicate manner.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: No one should be praised for his goodness if he has not strength enough to be wicked. All other goodness is but too often an idleness or powerlessness of will.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is not so dangerous to do wrong to most men, as to do them too much good.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Nothing flatters our pride so much as the confidence of the great, because we regard it as the result of our worth, without remembering that generally 'tis but vanity, or the inability to keep a secret.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We may say of conformity as distinguished from beauty, that it is a symmetry which knows no rules, and a secret harmony of features both one with each other and with the colour and appearance of the person.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We often bore others when we think we cannot possibly bore them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Few things are impossible in themselves; application to make them succeed fails us more often than the means.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Sovereign ability consists in knowing the value of things.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There is great ability in knowing how to conceal one's ability.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: What seems generosity is often disguised ambition, that despises small to run after greater interest.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The fidelity of most men is merely an invention of self-love to win confidence; a method to place us above others and to render us depositaries of the most important matters.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Magnanimity despises all, to win all.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There is no less eloquence in the voice, in the eyes and in the air of a speaker than in his choice of words.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: True eloquence consists in saying all that should be, not all that could be said.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are people whose faults become them, others whose very virtues disgrace them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is as common to change one's tastes, as it is uncommon to change one's inclinations.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Interest sets at work all sorts of virtues and vices.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: All feelings have their peculiar tone of voice, gestures and looks, and this harmony, as it is good or bad, pleasant or unpleasant, makes people agreeable or disagreeable.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: In all professions we affect a part and an appearance to seem what we wish to be. Thus the world is merely composed of actors.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Gravity is a mysterious carriage of the body invented to conceal the want of mind.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Good taste arises more from judgment than wit.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The pleasure of love is in loving, we are happier in the passion we feel than in that we inspire.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Civility is but a desire to receive civility, and to be esteemed polite.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The usual education of young people is to inspire them with a second self-love.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There is no passion wherein self-love reigns so powerfully as in love, and one is always more ready to sacrifice the peace of the loved one than his own.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: What we call liberality is often but the vanity of giving, which we like more than that we give away.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Pity is often a reflection of our own evils in the ills of others. It is a delicate foresight of the troubles into which we may fall. We help others that on like occasions we may be helped ourselves, and these services which we render, are in reality benefits we confer on ourselves by anticipation.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: A narrow mind begets obstinacy, and we do not easily believe what we cannot see.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We deceive ourselves if we believe that there are violent passions like ambition and love that can triumph over others. Idleness, languishing as she is, does not often fail in being mistress; she usurps authority over all the plans and actions of life; imperceptibly consuming and destroying both passions and virtues.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: A quickness in believing evil without having sufficiently examined it, is the effect of pride and laziness. We wish to find the guilty, and we do not wish to trouble ourselves in examining the crime.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We credit judges with the meanest motives, and yet we desire our reputation and fame should depend upon the judgment of men, who are all, either from their jealousy or pre-occupation or want of intelligence, opposed to us—and yet 'tis only to make these men decide in our favour that we peril in so many ways both our peace and our life.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: No man is clever enough to know all the evil he does.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: One honour won is a surety for more.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Youth is a continual intoxication; it is the fever of reason.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Nothing should so humiliate men who have deserved great praise, as the care they have taken to acquire it by the smallest means.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are persons of whom the world approves who have no merit beyond the vices they use in the affairs of life.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The beauty of novelty is to love as the flower to the fruit; it lends a lustre which is easily lost, but which never returns.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Natural goodness, which boasts of being so apparent, is often smothered by the least interest.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Absence extinguishes small passions and increases great ones, as the wind will blow out a candle, and blow in a fire.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: What makes us so often discontented with those who transact business for us is that they almost always abandon the interest of their friends for the interest of the business, because they wish to have the honour of succeeding in that which they have undertaken.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: When we exaggerate the tenderness of our friends towards us, it is often less from gratitude than from a desire to exhibit our own merit.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The praise we give to new comers into the world arises from the envy we bear to those who are established.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Pride, which inspires, often serves to moderate envy.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Some disguised lies so resemble truth, that we should judge badly were we not deceived.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Sometimes there is not less ability in knowing how to use than in giving good advice.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are wicked people who would be much less dangerous if they were wholly without goodness.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Magnanimity is sufficiently defined by its name, nevertheless one can say it is the good sense of pride, the most noble way of receiving praise.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is impossible to love a second time those whom we have really ceased to love.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Fertility of mind does not furnish us with so many resources on the same matter, as the lack of intelligence makes us hesitate at each thing our imagination presents, and hinders us from at first discerning which is the best.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are matters and maladies which at certain times remedies only serve to make worse; true skill consists in knowing when it is dangerous to use them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Affected simplicity is refined imposture.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are as many errors of temper as of mind.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Man's merit, like the crops, has its season.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: One may say of temper as of many buildings; it has divers aspects, some agreeable, others disagreeable.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Moderation cannot claim the merit of opposing and overcoming Ambition: they are never found together. Moderation is the languor and sloth of the soul, Ambition its activity and heat.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We always like those who admire us, we do not always like those whom we admire.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is well that we know not all our wishes.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is difficult to love those we do not esteem, but it is no less so to love those whom we esteem much more than ourselves.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Bodily temperaments have a common course and rule which imperceptibly affect our will. They advance in combination, and successively exercise a secret empire over us, so that, without our perceiving it, they become a great part of all our actions.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The gratitude of most men is but a secret desire of receiving greater benefits.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Almost all the world takes pleasure in paying small debts; many people show gratitude for trifling, but there is hardly one who does not show ingratitude for great favours.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are follies as catching as infections.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Many people despise, but few know how to bestow wealth.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Only in things of small value we usually are bold enough not to trust to appearances.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Whatever good quality may be imputed to us, we ourselves find nothing new in it.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We may forgive those who bore us, we cannot forgive those whom we bore.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Interest which is accused of all our misdeeds often should be praised for our good deeds.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We find very few ungrateful people when we are able to confer favours.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is as proper to be boastful alone as it is ridiculous to be so in company.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Moderation is made a virtue to limit the ambition of the great; to console ordinary people for their small fortune and equally small ability.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are persons fated to be fools, who commit follies not only by choice, but who are forced by fortune to do so.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Sometimes there are accidents in our life the skilful extrication from which demands a little folly.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: If there be men whose folly has never appeared, it is because it has never been closely looked for.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Lovers are never tired of each other,—they always speak of themselves.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: How is it that our memory is good enough to retain the least triviality that happens to us, and yet not good enough to recollect how often we have told it to the same person?
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The extreme delight we take in talking of ourselves should warn us that it is not shared by those who listen.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: What commonly hinders us from showing the recesses of our heart to our friends, is not the distrust we have of them, but that we have of ourselves.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: 'Tis a small misfortune to oblige an ungrateful man; but it is unbearable to be obliged by a scoundrel.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We may find means to cure a fool of his folly, but there are none to set straight a cross-grained spirit.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: If we take the liberty to dwell on their faults we cannot long preserve the feelings we should hold towards our friends and benefactors.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: To praise princes for virtues they do not possess is but to reproach them with impunity.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We are nearer loving those who hate us, than those who love us more than we desire.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Those only are despicable who fear to be despised.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Our wisdom is no less at the mercy of Fortune than our goods.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There is more self-love than love in jealousy.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We often comfort ourselves by the weakness of evils, for which reason has not the strength to console us.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Ridicule dishonours more than dishonour itself.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We own to small faults to persuade others that we have not great ones.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Envy is more irreconcilable than hatred.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We believe, sometimes, that we hate flattery —we only dislike the method.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We pardon in the degree that we love.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is more difficult to be faithful to a mistress when one is happy, than when we are ill-treated by her.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: In love deceit almost always goes further than mistrust.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There is a kind of love, the excess of which forbids jealousy.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are certain good qualities as there are senses, and those who want them can neither perceive nor understand them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: When our hatred is too bitter it places us below those whom we hate.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We only appreciate our good or evil in proportion to our self-love.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The heat of youth is not more opposed to safety than the coldness of age.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The accent of our native country dwells in the heart and mind as well as on the tongue.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: To be a great man one should know how to profit by every phase of fortune.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Most men, like plants, possess hidden qualities which chance discovers.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Opportunity makes us known to others, but more to ourselves.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We hardly find any persons of good sense, save those who agree with us.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: When one loves one doubts even what one most believes.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The greatest miracle of love is to eradicate flirtation.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Why we hate with so much bitterness those who deceive us is because they think themselves more clever than we are.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We have much trouble to break with one, when we no longer are in love.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We almost always are bored with persons with whom we should not be bored.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: A gentleman may love like a lunatic, but not like a beast.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are certain defects which well mounted glitter like virtue itself.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Sometimes we lose friends for whose loss our regret is greater than our grief, and others for whom our grief is greater than our regret.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Usually we only praise heartily those who admire us.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Little minds are too much wounded by little things; great minds see all and are not even hurt.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Humility is the true proof of Christian virtues; without it we retain all our faults, and they are only covered by pride to hide them from others, and often from ourselves.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Infidelities should extinguish love, and we ought not to be jealous when we have cause to be so. No persons escape causing jealousy who are worthy of exciting it.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We are more humiliated by the least infidelity towards us, than by our greatest towards others.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Jealousy is always born with love, but does not always die with it.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The evils we do to others give us less pain than those we do to ourselves.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We well know that it is bad taste to talk of our wives; but we do not so well know that it is the same to speak of ourselves.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are virtues which degenerate into vices when they arise from Nature, and others which when acquired are never perfect. For example, reason must teach us to manage our estate and our confidence, while Nature should have given us goodness and valour.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: However we distrust the sincerity of those whom we talk with, we always believe them more sincere with us than with others.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The violences we put upon ourselves to escape love are often more cruel than the cruelty of those we love.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There are not many cowards who know the whole of their fear.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is generally the fault of the loved one not to perceive when love ceases.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Most young people think they are natural when they are only boorish and rude.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Some tears after having deceived others deceive ourselves.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Ordinary men commonly condemn what is beyond them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Envy is destroyed by true friendship, flirtation by true love.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The greatest mistake of penetration is not to have fallen short, but to have gone too far.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We may bestow advice, but we cannot inspire the conduct.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: As our merit declines so also does our taste.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Fortune makes visible our virtues or our vices, as light does objects.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The struggle we undergo to remain faithful to one we love is little better than infidelity.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Our actions are like the rhymed ends of blank verses (Bouts-Rimes) where to each one puts what construction he pleases.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The desire of talking about ourselves, and of putting our faults in the light we wish them to be seen, forms a great part of our sincerity.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We should only be astonished at still being able to be astonished.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is equally as difficult to be contented when one has too much or too little love.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: No people are more often wrong than those who will not allow themselves to be wrong.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: A fool has not stuff in him to be good.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: If vanity does not overthrow all virtues, at least she makes them totter.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: What makes the vanity of others unsupportable is that it wounds our own.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We give up more easily our interest than our taste.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Fortune appears so blind to none as to those to whom she has done no good.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We should manage fortune like our health, enjoy it when it is good, be patient when it is bad, and never resort to strong remedies but in an extremity.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Awkwardness sometimes disappears in the camp, never in the court.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: A man is often more clever than one other, but not than all others.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We are often less unhappy at being deceived by one we loved, than on being deceived.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We keep our first lover for a long time—if we do not get a second.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We have not the courage to say generally that we have no faults, and that our enemies have no good qualities; but in fact we are not far from believing so.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Of all our faults that which we most readily admit is idleness: we believe that it makes all virtues ineffectual, and that without utterly destroying, it at least suspends their operation.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There is a kind of greatness which does not depend upon fortune: it is a certain manner what distinguishes us, and which seems to destine us for great things; it is the value we insensibly set upon ourselves; it is by this quality that we gain the deference of other men, and it is this which commonly raises us more above them, than birth, rank, or even merit itself.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There may be talent without position, but there is no position without some kind of talent.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: What we find the least of in flirtation is love.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Fortune sometimes uses our faults to exalt us, and there are tiresome people whose deserts would be ill rewarded if we did not desire to purchase their absence.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It appears that nature has hid at the bottom of our hearts talents and abilities unknown to us. It is only the passions that have the power of bringing them to light, and sometimes give us views more true and more perfect than art could possibly do.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We reach quite inexperienced the different stages of life, and often, in spite of the number of our years, we lack experience.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It may well be that those who have trapped us by their tricks do not seem to us so foolish as we seem to ourselves when trapped by the tricks of others.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The most dangerous folly of old persons who have been loveable is to forget that they are no longer so.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We should often be ashamed of our very best actions if the world only saw the motives which caused them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The greatest effort of friendship is not to show our faults to a friend, but to show him his own.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Whatever disgrace we may have deserved, it is almost always in our power to re-establish our character.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: A man cannot please long who has only one kind of wit.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Idiots and lunatics see only their own wit.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Wit sometimes enables us to act rudely with impunity.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The vivacity which increases in old age is not far removed from folly.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: In love the quickest is always the best cure.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We may seem great in a post beneath our capacity, but we oftener seem little in a post above it.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We often believe we have constancy in misfortune when we have nothing but debasement, and we suffer misfortunes without regarding them as cowards who let themselves be killed from fear of defending themselves.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Conceit causes more conversation than wit.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: All passions make us commit some faults, love alone makes us ridiculous.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We often credit ourselves with vices the reverse of what we have, thus when weak we boast of our obstinacy.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Penetration has a spice of divination in it which tickles our vanity more than any other quality of the mind.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The charm of novelty and old custom, however opposite to each other, equally blind us to the faults of our friends.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Most friends sicken us of friendship, most devotees of devotion.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We easily forgive in our friends those faults we do not perceive.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: In the old age of love as in life we still survive for the evils, though no longer for the pleasures.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Nothing prevents our being unaffected so much as our desire to seem so.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: To praise good actions heartily is in some measure to take part in them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The most certain sign of being born with great qualities is to be born without envy.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: When our friends have deceived us we owe them but indifference to the tokens of their friendship, yet for their misfortunes we always owe them pity.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: It is far easier to know men than to know man.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We should not judge of a man's merit by his great abilities, but by the use he makes of them.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: There is a certain lively gratitude which not only releases us from benefits received, but which also, by making a return to our friends as payment, renders them indebted to us.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We should earnestly desire but few things if we clearly knew what we desired.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: As in friendship so in love, we are often happier from ignorance than from knowledge.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: We try to make a virtue of vices we are loth to correct.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
work: Reflections; or, Sentences and Moral Maxims
translator: J. W. Willis Bund & J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: The most violent passions give some respite, but vanity always disturbs us.
author: François de La Rochefoucauld
