text: What is the present estate of my understanding? For herein lieth all indeed. As for all other things, they are without the compass of mine own will: and if without the compass of my will, then are they as dead things unto me, and as it were mere smoke.
author: Marcus Aurelius

text: Death is nothing to us; for the body, when it has been resolved into its elements, has no feeling, and that which has no feeling is nothing to us.
author: Epicurus

text: The magnitude of pleasure reaches its limit in the removal of all pain. When pleasure is present, so long as it is uninterrupted, there is no pain either of body or of mind or of both together.
author: Epicurus

text: Continuous pain does not last long in the body; on the contrary, pain, if extreme, is present a short time, and even that degree of pain which barely outweighs pleasure in the body does not last for many days together. Illnesses of long duration even permit of an excess of pleasure over pain in the body.
author: Epicurus

text: It is impossible to live a pleasant life without living wisely and well and justly, and it is impossible to live wisely and well and justly without living pleasantly. Whenever any one of these is lacking, when, for instance, the person is not able to live wisely, though he lives well and justly, it is impossible for him to live a pleasant life.
author: Epicurus

text: In order to obtain security from other people any means whatever of procuring this was a natural good.
author: Epicurus

text: Some people have sought to become famous and renowned, thinking that thus they would make themselves secure against their fellow-humans. If, then, the life of such persons really was secure, they attained natural good; if, however, it was insecure, they have not attained the end which by nature's own prompting they originally sought.
author: Epicurus

text: No pleasure is in itself evil, but the things which produce certain pleasures entail annoyances many times greater than the pleasures themselves.
author: Epicurus

text: If all pleasure had been capable of accumulation, — if this had gone on not only be recurrences in time, but all over the frame or, at any rate, over the principal parts of human nature, there would never have been any difference between one pleasure and another, as in fact there is.
author: Epicurus

text: If we had never been molested by alarms at celestial and atmospheric phenomena, nor by the misgiving that death somehow affects us, nor by neglect of the proper limits of pains and desires, we should have had no need to study natural science.
author: Epicurus

text: It would be impossible to banish fear on matters of the highest importance, if a person did not know the nature of the whole universe, but lived in dread of what the legends tell us. Hence without the study of nature there was no enjoyment of unmixed pleasures.
author: Epicurus

text: There would be no advantage in providing security against our fellow humans, so long as we were alarmed by occurrences over our heads or beneath the earth or in general by whatever happens in the boundless universe.
author: Epicurus

text: When tolerable security against our fellow humans is attained, then on a basis of power sufficient to afford supports and of material prosperity arises in most genuine form the security of a quiet private life withdrawn from the multitude.
author: Epicurus

text: Nature's wealth at once has its bounds and is easy to procure; but the wealth of vain fancies recedes to an infinite distance.
author: Epicurus

text: Fortune but seldom interferes with the wise person; his greatest and highest interests have been, are, and will be, directed by reason throughout the course of his life.
author: Epicurus

text: The just person enjoys. the greatest peace of mind, while the unjust is full of the utmost disquietude.
author: Epicurus

text: Pleasure in the body admits no increase when once the pain of want has been removed; after that it only admits of variation. The limit of pleasure in the mind, however, is reached when we reflect on the things themselves and their congeners which cause the mind the greatest alarms.
author: Epicurus

text: Unlimited time and limited time afford an equal amount of pleasure, if we measure the limits of that pleasure by reason.
author: Epicurus

text: He who understands the limits of life knows how easy it is to procure enough to remove the pain of want and make the whole of life complete and perfect. Hence he has no longer any need of things which are not to be won save by labor and conflict.
author: Epicurus

text: We must take into account as the end all that really exists and all clear evidence of sense to which we refer our opinions; for otherwise everything will be full of uncertainty and confusion.
author: Epicurus

text: If you fight against all your sensations, you will have no standard to which to refer, and thus no means of judging even those judgments which you pronounce false.
author: Epicurus

text: If you do not on every separate occasion refer each of your actions to the end prescribed by nature, but instead of this in the act of choice or avoidance swerve aside to some other end, your acts will not be consistent with your theories.
author: Epicurus

text: All such desires as lead to no pain when they remain ungratified are unnecessary, and the longing is easily got rid of, when the thing desired is difficult to procure or when the desires seem likely to produce harm.
author: Epicurus

text: Of all the means which are procured by wisdom to ensure happiness throughout the whole of life, by far the most important is the acquisition of friends.
author: Epicurus

text: The same conviction which inspires confidence that nothing we have to fear is eternal or even of long duration, also enables us to see that even in our limited conditions of life nothing enhances our security so much as friendship.
author: Epicurus

text: Of our desires some are natural and necessary others are natural, but not necessary; others, again, are neither natural nor necessary, but are due to illusory opinion.
author: Epicurus

text: Those natural desires which entail no pain when not gratified, though their objects are vehemently pursued, are also due to illusory opinion; and when they are not got rid of, it is not because of their own nature, but because of the person's illusory opinion.
author: Epicurus

text: Natural justice is a symbol or expression of usefullness, to prevent one person from harming or being harmed by another.
author: Epicurus

text: Those animals which are incapable of making covenants with one another, to the end that they may neither inflict nor suffer harm, are without either justice or injustice. And those tribes which either could not or would not form mutual covenants to the same end are in like case.
author: Epicurus

text: There never was an absolute justice, but only an agreement made in reciprocal association in whatever localities now and again from time to time, providing against the infliction or suffering of harm.
author: Epicurus

text: Injustice is not in itself an evil, but only in its consequence, viz. the terror which is excited by apprehension that those appointed to punish such offenses will discover the injustice.
author: Epicurus

text: It is impossible for the person who secretly violates any article of the social compact to feel confident that he will remain undiscovered, even if he has already escaped ten thousand times; for right on to the end of his life he is never sure he will not be detected.
author: Epicurus

text: Taken generally, justice is the same for all, to wit, something found useful in mutual association; but in its application to particular cases of locality or conditions of whatever kind, it varies under different circumstances.
author: Epicurus

text: He who best knew how to meet fear of external foes made into one family all the creatures he could; and those he could not, he at any rate did not treat as aliens; and where he found even this impossible, he avoided all association, and, so far as was useful, kept them at a distance.
author: Epicurus

text: The art of association then becomes, as I have said before, the mother of action, studied and applied by all.
author: Alexis de Tocqueville

text: If men are to remain civilized, or to become so, the art of associating together must grow and improve in the same ratio in which the equality of conditions is increased.
author: Alexis de Tocqueville

text: Truths are truths only in relation to a particular mankind.
author: Oswald Spengler
work: The Decline of the West, vol. I

text: Each Culture has its own new possibilities of self-expression which arise, ripen, decay, and never return.
author: Oswald Spengler
work: The Decline of the West, vol. I

text: From the beginning of history, there has been no human society, however small, that has not contained the germ of every vice.
author: Arthur de Gobineau
note: A historical author’s claim, excerpted from his argument about the causes of social decline.

text: All systems of power are, at their origin, mixed up with force.
author: François Guizot
work: General History of Civilisation in Europe
translator: Chambers edition (1848); translator unnamed in this edition

text: The excess of liberty, whether in States or individuals, seems only to pass into excess of slavery.
author: Plato
note: Socrates speaking in Plato’s dialogue, during the argument about democracy and tyranny.

text: I neither know nor think that I know.
author: Socrates
note: Socrates as portrayed by Plato. This is a reported speech, not a surviving text written by Socrates.

text: The unexamined life is not worth living.
author: Socrates
note: Socrates as portrayed by Plato. Excerpt from a longer sentence; initial letter capitalized.

text: What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not.
author: Saint Augustine
note: Excerpt; the source continues after a colon.

text: And Covenants, without the Sword, are but Words, and of no strength to secure a man at all.
author: Thomas Hobbes

text: For words are wise mens counters, they do but reckon by them: but they are the mony of fooles, that value them by the authority of an Aristotle, a Cicero, or a Thomas, or any other Doctor whatsoever, if but a man.
author: Thomas Hobbes
note: Original spelling retained.

text: Speaking is half his who speaks, and half his who hears.
author: Michel de Montaigne
reference: Book III, chapter XIII · Of Experience
translator: Charles Cotton; edited by W. C. Hazlitt (1877)
note: Excerpt; the source continues after a semicolon.

text: Man is sometimes extraordinarily, passionately, in love with suffering, and that is a fact.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
note: The Underground Man speaking. A fictional narrator’s claim, not an unqualified statement of the author’s beliefs.

text: You know the direct, legitimate fruit of consciousness is inertia, that is, conscious sitting-with-the-hands-folded.
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
note: The Underground Man speaking; fictional, deliberately unreliable narration.

text: A king is history’s slave.
author: Leo Tolstoy

text: History, that is, the unconscious, general, hive life of mankind, uses every moment of the life of kings as a tool for its own purposes.
author: Leo Tolstoy

text: Observe due measure: and proportion is best in all things.
author: Hesiod

text: Fools! They know not how much more the half is than the whole, nor what great advantage there is in mallow and asphodel.
author: Hesiod
note: An image of modest sufficiency in Hesiod’s rebuke to unjust judges. Editorial footnote marker omitted.

text: Dreams are very curious and unaccountable things, and they do not by any means invariably come true.
author: Homer
note: Penelope speaking to the disguised Odysseus. Excerpt; initial letter capitalized.

text: The growth of the power of Athens, and the alarm which this inspired in Lacedaemon, made war inevitable.
author: Thucydides
note: Thucydides’ interpretation of the cause of the Peloponnesian War.

text: Words had to change their ordinary meaning and to take that which was now given them.
author: Thucydides
note: On the corruption of political language during civil strife at Corcyra.

text: The strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must.
author: Thucydides
note: The Athenian envoys speaking in Thucydides’ account. Excerpt; initial letter capitalized.

text: In most cases men willingly believe what they wish.
author: Julius Caesar
note: Excerpt; initial letter capitalized.

text: He who is obliged to become a soldier must also, so long as the state is not rotten, have it in his power to become an officer.
author: Theodor Mommsen
work: The History of Rome, book I
reference: Chapter VI · The Non-Burgesses and the Reformed Constitution
note: Excerpt from Mommsen’s argument about military obligation and political rights; source continues after a semicolon.

text: For that which is common to the greatest number has the least care bestowed upon it.
author: Aristotle

text: Every one thinks chiefly of his own, hardly at all of the common interest; and only when he is himself concerned as an individual.
author: Aristotle

text: Wear not, then, one mood only in thyself; think not that thy word, and thine alone, must be right.
author: Sophocles
note: Haemon speaking to Creon; dramatic dialogue.

text: Wisdom is the supreme part of happiness; and reverence towards the gods must be inviolate.
author: Sophocles
note: The Chorus speaking in the play’s conclusion.

text: At last I understand the awful deed I am to do; but passion, that cause of direst woes to mortal man, hath triumphed o'er my sober thoughts.
author: Euripides
note: Medea speaking before killing her children; a tragic portrayal of the conflict between judgment and passion.

text: Logistically accelerating techno-economic interactivity crumbles social order in auto-sophisticating machine runaway.
author: Nick Land
translator: Original English; Urbanomic publisher excerpt (2011 edition)

text: We need decentralization because only thus can we insure that the knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place will be promptly used.
author: Friedrich Hayek
work: The Use of Knowledge in Society

text: Society is concerted action, cooperation. Society is the outcome of conscious and purposeful behavior.
author: Ludwig von Mises

text: No concept man forms is valid unless he integrates it without contradiction into the total sum of his knowledge.
author: Ayn Rand
work: For the New Intellectual · Galt’s Speech
translator: Original English (1961); authorized excerpt in Ayn Rand Lexicon
note: A statement from the fictional character John Galt’s speech, reprinted in For the New Intellectual.

text: If no other, at least this, that I am prepared for every kind of fortune.
author: Diogenes
work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers
note: Reported by Diogenes Laertius as Diogenes’ answer when asked what advantage he had derived from philosophy.

text: That child has beaten me in simplicity.
author: Diogenes
work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers
note: Reported by Diogenes Laertius: Diogenes discards his cup after seeing a child drink from its hands.

text: Make haste slowly.
author: Caesar Augustus
note: A Greek proverb that Suetonius says Augustus frequently used; not claimed as an original saying coined by Augustus.

text: That state which in ignorance of its power goes to war with a stronger than itself ends by being uprooted or else reduced to slavery.
author: Xenophon
note: Socrates speaking, as recorded in Xenophon’s dialogue.

text: Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.
author: Arthur C. Clarke
translator: Original English; quotation reproduced by the Arthur C. Clarke Foundation
note: The author’s foundation reproduces this maxim; the link opens that official excerpt.

text: Of practical wisdom these are the three fruits: to deliberate well, to speak to the point, to do what is right.
author: Democritus
work: Fragments · Source Book in Ancient Philosophy
note: A transmitted fragment, preserved in the later collection attributed to Democritus; not a surviving complete book.

text: By convention sweet is sweet, by convention bitter is bitter, by convention hot is hot, by convention cold is cold, by convention color is color. But in reality there are atoms and the void.
author: Democritus
work: Fragments · Source Book in Ancient Philosophy
reference: Fragment 9 · Sextus Empiricus, Against the Mathematicians VII.135
note: Reported by Sextus Empiricus. The Greek gloss following “convention” is omitted.

text: Train yourself in self-imposed toils, that you may be able to endure those which others impose upon you.
author: Isocrates
note: Traditionally attributed to Isocrates; the authorship of To Demonicus is disputed.

text: Consider that you owe it to yourself no less to mistrust bad men than to put your trust in the good.
author: Isocrates
note: Traditionally attributed to Isocrates; the authorship of To Demonicus is disputed.

text: It must be borne in mind that my design is not to write histories, but lives.
author: Plutarch
translator: John Dryden translation, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough (1859)
note: Plutarch’s distinction between biography and the narration of great public events.

text: Each person is only their dream of themselves.
author: Fernando Pessoa
reference: Fragment beginning “Não sei quem sou, que alma tenho”
note: Bernardo Soares, Pessoa’s literary persona, speaking. Fragment numbering varies between editions.
original: Cada pessoa é apenas o seu sonho de si próprio.

text: I am a character in my own dramas.
author: Fernando Pessoa
reference: Fragment beginning “Não sei quem sou, que alma tenho”
note: Bernardo Soares, Pessoa’s literary persona, speaking. Fragment numbering varies between editions.
original: Sou uma personagem de dramas meus.

text: Giving what you do not have, you acquire what you knew how to give from the emptiness of your being.
author: Nicolae Steinhardt
work: Dăruind vei dobândi (Giving, You Shall Receive)
note: An editorial English translation of the Romanian source excerpt; not a quotation from a published English edition.
original: dand ceea ce nu ai, dobandesti ceea ce ai stiut sa dai din golul fiintei tale.

text: People first feel without noticing, then notice with a troubled and agitated spirit, and finally reflect with a clear mind.
author: Giambattista Vico
reference: Book I, section II, axiom LIII · §218
translator: Marginalia editorial translation from Italian; 1744 text, Nicolini edition (1928)
note: Editorial English translation. The linked page also gives the Italian text.
original: Gli uomini prima sentono senz’avvertire, dappoi avvertiscono con animo perturbato e commosso, finalmente riflettono con mente pura.

text: The most stimulating challenge is to be found in a mean between a deficiency of severity and an excess of it.
author: Arnold J. Toynbee
translator: English; challenge-and-response excerpt reproduced by Panarchy
note: A proposed hypothesis in Toynbee’s argument, not an established law. Excerpt; initial letter capitalized.

text: Sometimes doing nothing is the most violent thing to do.
author: Slavoj Žižek
translator: Original English; spoken discussion, Politics and Prose (2008)
note: Žižek’s spoken summary of his book’s argument. The source links the transcript and recording; wording follows the spoken version.

text: The various modes of worship, which prevailed in the Roman world, were all considered by the people, as equally true; by the philosopher, as equally false; and by the magistrate, as equally useful.
author: Edward Gibbon
work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
note: Gibbon’s interpretation of Roman religious toleration.

text: Politics is a strong and slow boring of hard boards. It takes both passion and perspective.
author: Max Weber
translator: H. H. Gerth and C. Wright Mills (1946)

text: Even the simple act which we describe as "seeing some one we know" is, to some extent, an intellectual process.
author: Marcel Proust
idea: Perception is partly constructed: our prior ideas help form the person we think we simply see.
note: The novel’s narrator reflecting on the family’s different pictures of Swann.

text: The facts of life do not penetrate to the sphere in which our beliefs are cherished; as it was not they that engendered those beliefs, so they are powerless to destroy them.
author: Marcel Proust
reference: Combray, II · Vinteuil and his daughter
idea: A belief sustained by emotional attachment may resist evidence because evidence was never what sustained it.
note: Narratorial observation, not a universal psychological law. Excerpt ends at a semicolon in the source.

text: As I find myself back of things, and that as mind, so I must later find myself also back of thoughts,—to wit, as their creator and owner.
author: Max Stirner
reference: Part I, chapter I · A Human Life; p. 16
idea: Stirner asks whether we can use our ideals as our creations, instead of accepting them as authorities over us.

text: Our own interest is again a marvellous instrument for nicely putting out our eyes.
author: Blaise Pascal
idea: Self-interest can alter what appears convincing before we consciously decide to be dishonest.

text: The rude beginnings of every art acquire a greater celebrity than the art in perfection.
author: Voltaire
idea: Priority and novelty can dominate collective reputation even when later work is technically better.
note: Excerpt ends at a semicolon; Voltaire illustrates it by contrasting early inventors with later masters.

text: I was thus led to infer that the ground of our opinions is far more custom and example than any certain knowledge.
author: René Descartes
translator: John Veitch; linked Project Gutenberg edition
idea: Disagreement across cultures exposes how much apparent certainty comes from imitation rather than justification.

text: It is precisely because the force of circumstances tends continually to destroy equality that the force of legislation should always tend to its maintenance.
author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
reference: Book II, chapter XI · The Various Systems of Legislation
idea: Equality is not a condition that maintains itself: Rousseau sees institutions as counterweights to forces that concentrate advantage.

text: Such negative criticism would indeed be poor enough as an ultimate result; but as a means to attaining any positive knowledge or conviction worthy the name, it cannot be valued too highly.
author: John Stuart Mill
reference: Chapter II · Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion
idea: Finding flaws is not yet a theory, but it is a necessary method for earning confidence in one.
note: “Such negative criticism” refers to exposing weaknesses in theories or errors in practice; excerpt ends at a semicolon.

text: This power to act according to discretion, for the public good, without the prescription of the law, and sometimes even against it, is that which is called prerogative.
author: John Locke
idea: General rules cannot anticipate every emergency. Locke permits executive discretion but ties its legitimacy to the public good.
note: Excerpt ends at a colon in the original.

text: There is, however, no such thing as private ownership established by nature.
author: Cicero
idea: Cicero treats ownership as established by social practices—occupation, agreement and law—rather than as a natural division of the earth.
note: Opening clause of a longer sentence. Cicero goes on to defend respecting property once established; this excerpt does not claim that he rejects property rights.

text: There is a great difference between the subject-matter of a benefit, and the benefit itself.
author: Seneca
idea: For Seneca the valuable object is only the vehicle of a gift; the benefit lies in the giver’s intention, so its worth is not reducible to its price.

text: What! if any savage, by a stern countenance and bare feet, and the texture of a scanty gown, should imitate Cato; will he represent the virtue and morals of Cato?
author: Horace
translator: Christopher Smart; revised by Theodore Alois Buckley
reference: Book I, Epistle XIX · To Maecenas
idea: Imitating the visible signals of excellence is easier than reproducing the qualities that made those signals meaningful.
note: A prose translation of verse; “Cato” is the austere Roman exemplar mocked by superficial imitators.

text: Therefore it must be inferred that good counsels, whencesoever they come, are born of the wisdom of the prince, and not the wisdom of the prince from good counsels.
author: Niccolò Machiavelli
reference: Chapter XXIII · How Flatterers Should Be Avoided
idea: Expert advice does not remove the need for judgment: the ruler must select advisers, question them and reconcile their competing interests.

text: Nature is full of infinite causes that have never occured in experience.
author: Leonardo da Vinci
work: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci
idea: Experience constrains a theory without exhausting nature: what we have observed need not include every possible cause.
note: Spelling “occured” follows the linked edition.

text: Experience never errs; it is only your judgments that err by promising themselves effects such as are not caused by your experiments.
author: Leonardo da Vinci
work: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci
idea: A failed prediction challenges the inference we drew from an experiment; blaming experience protects the mistaken model.

text: Hence the knowledge of every knower is ruled according to its own nature.
author: Thomas Aquinas
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province; Benziger edition
idea: Knowing depends on the capacities of the knower. Aquinas uses this principle to explain why a created intellect cannot naturally comprehend the divine essence.

text: We must not then add wings, but rather lead and ballast to the understanding, to prevent its jumping or flying.
author: Francis Bacon
translator: English edition edited by Joseph Devey; P. F. Collier & Son (1902)
idea: Bacon wants disciplined movement from observations to intermediate principles before broad theories: imaginative speed is not a substitute for controlled inference.
note: Excerpt ends before “which has not yet been done”; the omitted continuation calls this a condition of scientific progress.

text: A mental image is more often vivid, in proportion as it is associated with a greater number of other images.
author: Baruch Spinoza
idea: An idea recurs more readily when many associations can reactivate it. Spinoza places this account of memory inside his argument about gaining power over the emotions.

text: I say, then, that belief is nothing but a more vivid, lively, forcible, firm, steady conception of an object, than what the imagination alone is ever able to attain.
author: David Hume
reference: Section V, Part II · Sceptical Solution of These Doubts
idea: For Hume, believing differs from merely imagining partly in how forcefully an idea is felt, not because belief attaches a separate logical label to it.

text: The circumstances are what render every civil and political scheme beneficial or noxious to mankind.
author: Edmund Burke
work: Reflections on the Revolution in France
reference: Opening discussion of political principles and circumstances
idea: Burke evaluates an institution by its setting and consequences: abstract approval of liberty or government does not decide whether this particular arrangement works.

text: The light dove cleaving in free flight the thin air, whose resistance it feels, might imagine that her movements would be far more free and rapid in airless space.
author: Immanuel Kant
idea: What looks like a limit can also be a condition of success. Kant compares reason’s dependence on experience to flight’s dependence on resisting air.

text: This bare fact of certainty, however, is really and admittedly the abstractest and the poorest kind of truth.
author: G. W. F. Hegel
translator: J. B. Baillie; Marxists Internet Archive edition
idea: Immediate sensory certainty seems rich, yet saying only “it is” leaves the object almost unexplained. Hegel distinguishes feeling certain from having determinate knowledge.
note: “This bare fact” refers to the unelaborated certainty that a sensed thing exists.

text: Not merely to know, but according to thy knowledge to do, is thy vocation.
author: Johann Gottlieb Fichte
idea: Fichte turns from a spectator’s account of knowledge to practical agency: the demand to act gives the world significance that detached contemplation cannot supply.
note: The inner voice addressed to the narrator; a quotation within Fichte’s first-person philosophical exposition.

text: When we perceive the end in the beginning, we move faster than time.
author: Emil Cioran
translator: Richard Howard; Penguin publisher sample (2020 edition)
reference: Chapter I, p. 4 · paragraph on the disabused man
idea: Cioran depicts disillusionment as anticipating an undertaking’s disappointment before living through it, collapsing the emotional distance between possibility and outcome.
note: A sentence from a longer aphorism, not a literal claim about time.

text: The threat to man does not come in the first instance from the potentially lethal machines and apparatus of technology.
author: Martin Heidegger
reference: Discussion of Enframing and danger · p. 28
idea: Heidegger’s deeper concern is a way of seeing that reduces everything to usable resources, thereby crowding out other ways of understanding beings.

text: Our social science may make us very wise or clever as regards the means for any objectives we might choose.
author: Leo Strauss
reference: Introduction · excerpt on instrumental social science
idea: Strauss separates technical competence from justification of ends: knowing how to achieve a goal does not settle whether that goal deserves pursuit.

text: Our questions and answers are in part determined by the historical tradition in which we find ourselves.
author: Karl Jaspers
translator: English excerpt in Walter Kaufmann’s edited anthology; translator not identified on linked page
idea: Inquiry cannot begin from nowhere. Jaspers asks us to appropriate inherited thought actively rather than mistake its assumptions for timeless starting points.

text: But an effect can become a cause, reinforcing the original cause and producing the same effect in an intensified form, and so on indefinitely.
author: George Orwell
reference: Opening discussion of language and thought, paragraph 2
idea: Political habits corrupt language, and corrupted language then makes those habits easier to sustain: Orwell is describing a feedback loop.

text: A theory cannot be tested by the “realism” of its “assumptions”.
author: Milton Friedman
translator: Original English (1953); Essays in Positive Economics, 1966 printing
reference: IV · The Significance and Role of the “Assumptions” of a Theory, p. 23
idea: Friedman proposes judging a model by the predictions relevant to its purpose, not by whether every simplifying assumption resembles reality. This is his methodological position, not an uncontested rule.
note: Clause extracted from a longer sentence; initial letter capitalized.

text: Every ‘good’ scientific theory is a prohibition: it forbids certain things to happen.
author: Karl Popper
translator: Original English (1963); classroom reprint of chapter 1
reference: Chapter 1 · Science: Conjectures and Refutations, conclusion 3
idea: A theory earns empirical content by ruling out outcomes. If it can accommodate every possible observation, observation cannot expose it as mistaken.
note: Quotation marks normalized; line-break hyphenation removed.

text: Failings of the intelligence are incorrigible, since those who do not know, do not know themselves, and cannot therefore seek what they lack.
author: Baltasar Gracián
reference: § 176 · Have Knowledge, or know those that have Knowledge
idea: A gap in understanding can also conceal the need for help. Gracián treats knowing when to consult others as part of intelligence itself.
note: Historical maxim, not a scientific claim that people cannot learn. Spacing in the digitized edition normalized.

text: “This should have been done before,” said Scipio, “but not now, when you have taken the bit and the rider is in the saddle.”
author: Scipio Africanus
idea: The anecdote makes bargaining power depend on timing: terms available before a decisive loss of control may disappear afterward.
note: Reported reply to Antiochus about peace terms, in the collection traditionally attributed to Plutarch; not a surviving text by Scipio. Narrative attribution retained.

text: Fame, the great ill, from small beginnings grows: Swift from the first; and ev’ry moment brings New vigour to her flights, new pinions to her wings.
author: Virgil
reference: Book IV · the personification of Rumour
idea: Rumour acquires power through circulation: each repetition increases its reach. Here “Fame” means spreading report, not admirable reputation.
note: Narration during the Dido episode. Verse line breaks collapsed.

text: He knows not what he sees, but what he sees, by it is he inflamed; and the same mistake that deceives his eyes, provokes them.
author: Ovid
idea: Narcissus desires a reflection because he misrecognizes it. The error is part of what generates the desire, rather than merely an obstacle to satisfying it.
note: Narration of the Narcissus myth, not a statement by Narcissus.

text: instead of looking on discussion as a stumbling-block in the way of action, we think it an indispensable preliminary to any wise action at all.
author: Pericles
idea: Pericles presents deliberation as a condition of effective action: courage and reflection can reinforce each other.
note: Clause excerpt from the speech as composed and reported by Thucydides; not a verbatim transcript. Opening lowercase retained.

text: But I hold to it that if I make my friends rich they will be my treasures themselves, and far better guards too, for me and all we have, than if I set hired watchmen over my wealth.
author: Cyrus the Great
idea: Wealth distributed to allies can become a reserve of cooperation. Xenophon’s Cyrus treats durable relationships as a form of security and usable power.
note: Cyrus speaking to Croesus in Xenophon’s literary portrayal; not a verified historical utterance.

text: The image of war as armed combat merges into the more extended image of a gigantic labor process.
author: Ernst Jünger
translator: English excerpt reproduced by University of Chicago Press (2019); translator not named in excerpt
reference: 1930 essay · epigraph in Roy Scranton, Total Mobilization, p. vi
idea: Industrial war draws production, transport and civilian work into conflict. The battlefield becomes one part of a society organized for war.
note: Linked source is the publisher’s identified excerpt, rather than the complete essay.

text: If this myth is tragic, that is because its hero is conscious.
author: Albert Camus
idea: For Camus, the pause in which Sisyphus understands his condition matters as much as the repeated labour. Lucidity produces anguish but also makes a response to the absurd possible.

text: But do thou restrain thy thought from this way of inquiry, nor let habit by its much experience force thee to cast upon this way a wandering eye or sounding ear or tongue; but judge by argument the much disputed proof uttered by me.
author: Parmenides
reference: Proem in linked edition · DK B7.2–6
idea: Habit and sensory familiarity do not settle what can coherently be thought. The poem asks the listener to test an account through reasoning.
note: The goddess addresses the traveller in the poem. The linked edition groups these lines in its proem; modern fragment numbering differs.

text: When power is cemented by goodwill, and the interest of all who join in a war is the same, then men are willing to share the labour, to endure the misfortunes, and to stand fast.
author: Demosthenes
idea: A coalition survives setbacks more readily when its members share purposes. Demosthenes contrasts willing cooperation with the apparent strength of coercion.
note: An argument urging Athens to oppose Philip; a political claim made in a particular conflict.

text: These men teach, if one give them money, to conquer in speaking, right or wrong.
author: Aristophanes
reference: Opening dialogue · Strepsiades describes the Thinkery
idea: When argument becomes a purchased technique for victory, persuasion can separate from truth and justice. The comedy makes that separation attractive to a man trying to escape his debts.
note: Spoken by the fictional Strepsiades. The play’s comic portrayal of Socrates is not a reliable historical account of his teaching.

text: They consult when unable to dissemble; they determine when not liable to mistake.
author: Tacitus
translator: Revised Oxford translation, edition introduced by Edward Brooks, Jr.
idea: Tacitus separates candid discussion from sober decision: different conditions can serve the discovery of opinions and the judgment of them.
note: His account of Germanic councils, describing discussion while drinking followed by reconsideration the next day; not advice to drink or a verified general rule.

text: The greatest gift that in his largess God Creating made, and unto his own goodness Nearest conformed, and that which he doth prize Most highly, is the freedom of the will, Wherewith the creatures of intelligence Both all and only were and are endowed.
author: Dante Alighieri
idea: Beatrice’s argument explains the seriousness of a vow: freely promising something puts the will itself into the commitment. Freedom helps create obligation, rather than simply removing it.
note: Spoken by Beatrice in the poem. Verse line breaks collapsed.

text: For there are two main obstacles to the knowledge of things, modesty that casts a mist before the understanding, and fear that, having fancied a danger, dissuades us from the attempt.
author: Desiderius Erasmus
idea: Folly provocatively argues that fear of error can prevent the experience from which judgment grows. The satire tests the limits of caution without making recklessness a universal rule.
note: Spoken by the personification Folly; the satirical speaker must not be treated as a straightforward statement of Erasmus’s own beliefs.

text: Just as useless laws weaken necessary ones, laws that can be evaded weaken legislation.
author: Montesquieu
translator: Editorial translation from the French; original supplied
idea: An ineffective rule can damage confidence in the system of rules. Legislative design therefore includes the effect one law has on the credibility of others.
original: Comme les lois inutiles affoiblissent les lois nécessaires, celles qu’on peut éluder affoiblissent la législation.

text: that which appears enormous, when measured by the stunted scale of the old diplomatic ideas, is really nothing at all, in the actual order of society.
author: François-René de Chateaubriand
reference: Volume V · Book I, recollection of the conclave of 1829
idea: Institutions can retain an old scale of importance after public attention has shifted. Chateaubriand explains his diplomatic boldness partly by recognizing that mismatch.
note: Clause excerpt concerning his handling of papal exclusion; opening lowercase retained.

text: So far is character from being the work of reasoned choice and consideration that in any action the intellect has nothing to do but to present motives to the will.
author: Arthur Schopenhauer
idea: The intellect supplies motives, while a person’s character determines how those motives move the will. This is Schopenhauer’s account of agency, not an established scientific finding.

text: whereas faith does the opposite, to-wit, makes the movements to regain the finite after having made those of infinite resignation.
author: Søren Kierkegaard
translator: Lee M. Hollander (1923), in Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard
reference: Preliminary Expectoration · faith and infinite resignation
idea: Resignation gives up a finite good; faith, as the pseudonymous narrator describes it, also trusts in receiving it again. The distinction concerns a paradoxical commitment, not ordinary optimism.
note: Clause excerpt by Kierkegaard’s pseudonymous narrator Johannes de silentio. Opening lowercase retained.

text: This is because proceedings are generally kept secret not only from the public but also from the accused.
author: Franz Kafka
idea: The accused must act without access to the case against him. Kafka’s court turns dependence on an opaque procedure into a form of power.
note: Narration describing the fictional court; not a factual claim about all legal systems.

text: I call crystallisation the operation of the mind which, from everything which is presented to it, draws the conclusion that there are new perfections in the object of its love.
author: Stendhal
translator: Philip Sidney Woolf and Cecil N. Sidney Woolf (1915; reprinted 1920)
reference: Book I · chapter II, The Birth of Love
idea: Desire reorganizes evidence: unrelated experiences become reasons to admire the beloved. Stendhal’s “crystallisation” names an active construction of perceived perfection.

text: There exists no norm that is applicable to chaos.
author: Carl Schmitt
translator: George Schwab (1985; University of Chicago Press edition 2005)
idea: Schmitt argues that rules presuppose conditions in which they can operate. The political question then becomes who decides whether those normal conditions exist.

text: Formulas all begin by being full of substance; you may call them the skin, the articulation into shape, into limbs and skin, of a substance that is already there: they had not been there otherwise.
author: Thomas Carlyle
work: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History
reference: Lecture V · The Hero as Man of Letters
idea: A formula or institution can begin as the expression of living conviction and later become hollow. Carlyle asks whether its animating substance still exists.

text: It often becomes impossible, amidst mutual accusations, to determine on whom the blame or the punishment of a pernicious measure, or series of pernicious measures, ought really to fall.
author: Alexander Hamilton
reference: Federalist No. 70 · the unity of the executive
idea: Dividing executive authority can also diffuse responsibility. Hamilton defends a single executive partly because the public can identify whom to hold accountable.

text: We must not make a scarecrow of the law, Setting it up to fear the birds of prey, And let it keep one shape till custom make it Their perch, and not their terror.
author: William Shakespeare
idea: A threat that is never carried out can become something people learn to ignore. Angelo uses this argument for strict enforcement; the play later exposes the problems of his own authority.
note: Spoken by the fictional Angelo, not a direct declaration of Shakespeare’s political beliefs. Verse line breaks collapsed.

text: She stirs up even the shiftless to toil; for a man grows eager to work when he considers his neighbour, a rich man who hastens to plough and plant and put his house in good order; and neighbour vies with his neighbour as he hurries after wealth. This Strife is wholesome for men.
author: Hesiod
reference: Lines 11–24 · the two kinds of Strife
idea: Hesiod distinguishes destructive conflict from productive emulation. Seeing a neighbour prosper can turn rivalry into work, without making every form of competition beneficial.
note: “She” refers to the beneficial kind of Strife, contrasted in the preceding lines with the kind that brings war.

author: David Hume
text: When any opinion leads to absurdities, it is certainly false; but it is not certain that an opinion is false, because it is of dangerous consequence.
idea: An uncomfortable implication is not a refutation. Hume separates the logical status of a claim from the social consequences of accepting it.

author: David Hume
text: Such is the influence of custom, that, where it is strongest, it not only covers our natural ignorance, but even conceals itself, and seems not to take place, merely because it is found in the highest degree.
idea: The most habitual inference feels least like an inference. Familiarity can hide both what we do not know and the mental shortcut filling that gap.

author: John Stuart Mill
text: Truth gains more even by the errors of one who, with due study and preparation, thinks for himself, than by the true opinions of those who only hold them because they do not suffer themselves to think.
reference: Chapter II · Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion
idea: A correct answer passively inherited can be less intellectually valuable than a reasoned mistake. Inquiry develops the ability to correct oneself.

author: John Stuart Mill
text: There is the greatest difference between presuming an opinion to be true, because, with every opportunity for contesting it, it has not been refuted, and assuming its truth for the purpose of not permitting its refutation.
reference: Chapter II · Of the Liberty of Thought and Discussion
idea: Mill distinguishes surviving criticism from suppressing criticism. Only the first gives others a reason to trust a belief.

author: John Locke
text: It is not necessary, no, nor so much as convenient, that the legislative should be always in being; but absolutely necessary that the executive power should, because there is not always need of new laws to be made, but always need of execution of the laws that are made.
reference: Chapter XIII · Of the Subordination of the Powers of the Commonwealth
idea: Laws can be written intermittently; enforcing them is continuous. Locke uses this asymmetry to distinguish legislative from executive power.

author: John Locke
text: The liberty of man, in society, is to be under no other legislative power, but that established, by consent, in the commonwealth; nor under the dominion of any will, or restraint of any law, but what that legislative shall enact, according to the trust put in it.
idea: Civil liberty is not exemption from every rule: it requires authorized, public rules instead of dependence on another person’s arbitrary will.

author: Baruch Spinoza
text: Herefrom it follows, first, that men think themselves free inasmuch as they are conscious of their volitions and desires, and never even dream, in their ignorance, of the causes which have disposed them so to wish and desire.
idea: Awareness of wanting something does not reveal why we want it. Spinoza explains how ignorance of causes can be mistaken for freedom.

author: Baruch Spinoza
text: The power and increase of every passion, and its persistence in existing are not defined by the power, whereby we ourselves endeavour to persist in existing, but by the power of an external cause compared with our own.
idea: A passion’s strength depends on the external forces acting on us, not merely on how determined we are to resist it.

author: Francis Bacon
translator: English edition edited by Joseph Devey; P. F. Collier & Son (1902)
text: Truth is not to be sought in the good fortune of any particular conjuncture of time, which is uncertain, but in the light of nature and experience, which is eternal.
idea: Neither being ancient nor being fashionable establishes a claim. Bacon grounds inquiry in nature and experience rather than a fortunate historical reputation.

author: Francis Bacon
translator: English edition edited by Joseph Devey; P. F. Collier & Son (1902)
text: The human understanding, when any proposition has been once laid down (either from general admission and belief, or from the pleasure it affords), forces everything else to add fresh support and confirmation.
idea: Once a view becomes ours, the mind recruits evidence to defend it. Bacon treats this as an obstacle that methods of inquiry must actively counter.
note: Excerpt ends at a semicolon in the source.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: To tell the truth is useful to those to whom it is spoken, but disadvantageous to those who tell it, because it makes them disliked.
reference: Passage on the incentives against candour
idea: Truth can benefit its listener while costing its speaker affection or status. Pascal points to an incentive that systematically filters honest feedback.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: There are different degrees in this aversion to truth; but all may perhaps be said to have it in some degree, because it is inseparable from self-love.
idea: Resistance to truth is not confined to unusually dishonest people. Pascal locates a more general source in our wish to preserve a flattering self-image.

author: Michel de Montaigne
translator: Charles Cotton; edited by W. C. Hazlitt (1877)
text: Whereas the passions which wholly reside in the soul, as ambition, avarice, and the rest, find the reason much more to do, because it cannot there be helped but by its own means; neither are those appetites capable of satiety, but grow sharper and increase by fruition.
reference: Book II, chapter XXXIII · The Story of Spurina
idea: Bodily appetites can be satisfied, but ambitions of the mind can expand as they are fulfilled. Accumulation can sharpen desire rather than end it.

author: Michel de Montaigne
translator: Charles Cotton; edited by W. C. Hazlitt (1877)
text: In plain truth, the cares and expense our parents are at in our education, point at nothing, but to furnish our heads with knowledge; but not a word of judgment and virtue.
idea: An education can stock the memory while neglecting the ability to judge or live well. Montaigne asks what knowledge actually equips a person to do.

author: Immanuel Kant
text: For example, the proposition, “Every change has a cause,” is a proposition à priori, but impure, because change is a conception which can only be derived from experience.
reference: Introduction · Of the Difference between Pure and Empirical Knowledge
idea: A claim can assert necessity while still using a concept learned from experience. Kant distinguishes a priori judgment from wholly pure a priori knowledge.

author: Immanuel Kant
text: Space, therefore, cannot be regarded as absolutely and in itself something determinative of the existence of things, because it is not itself an object, but only the form of possible objects.
reference: Transcendental Dialectic · First Antinomy, observations on the antithesis
idea: Kant treats space as a form in which objects can appear to us, rather than another object existing alongside them.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: Their rights do not rest upon their powers, because Right is of a moral complexion; they rest on the fact that the same will to live shows itself in every man at the same stage of its manifestation.
reference: Passage on the basis of equal rights
idea: Schopenhauer separates moral standing from differences in ability. Equal rights rest, in this argument, on the same will to live appearing in each person.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: They hold them sacred for the simple reason that those institutions and customs are not the invention of an idle head, but have grown up gradually by the force of circumstance and the wisdom of life itself, and are therefore suited to them as a nation.
reference: Passage on institutions as accumulated adaptation
idea: Customs can contain adjustments learned through experience even when nobody designed them as a complete system. This is an argument for examining their history before replacing them.

author: René Descartes
translator: John Veitch; linked Project Gutenberg edition
text: My present design, then, is not to teach the method which each ought to follow for the right conduct of his reason, but solely to describe the way in which I have endeavored to conduct my own.
idea: Descartes presents the method as an account of his own inquiry. Its value is to be examined, not accepted simply because he asserts authority.

author: René Descartes
translator: John Veitch; linked Project Gutenberg edition
text: On the other hand, when too much time is occupied in traveling, we become strangers to our native country; and the over curious in the customs of the past are generally ignorant of those of the present.
idea: The comparison between travel and historical reading makes a limit visible: acquiring one kind of understanding can displace attention to one’s present circumstances.

author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
text: Each man alienates, I admit, by the social compact, only such part of his powers, goods and liberty as it is important for the community to control; but it must also be granted that the Sovereign is sole judge of what is important.
reference: Book II, chapter IV · The Limits of the Sovereign Power
idea: The compact appears to reserve private liberty, yet the sovereign decides what the common interest requires. Rousseau exposes the difficult boundary between individual rights and collective authority.

author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
work: Discourse on the Origin of Inequality
text: Here all private persons return to their first equality, because they are nothing; and, subjects having no law but the will of their master, and their master no restraint but his passions, all notions of good and all principles of equity again vanish.
idea: People can become equal through shared powerlessness. Rousseau distinguishes that levelling from equality among free citizens.

author: Thomas Hobbes
text: For to know, who knowes the Rules almost of any Art, is a great degree of the knowledge of the same Art; because no man can be assured of the truth of anothers Rules, but he that is first taught to understand them.
reference: Part II, chapter XXX · Of the Office of the Soveraign Representative
idea: Judging an expert’s rules itself requires some understanding of the field. Hobbes identifies a difficulty in delegating judgment to authorities.

author: Alexis de Tocqueville
text: Not only is common opinion the only guide which private judgment retains amongst a democratic people, but amongst such a people it possesses a power infinitely beyond what it has elsewhere.
reference: Part I, chapter II · The principal source of belief
idea: Equality can weaken individual authorities while strengthening the authority of public opinion. Intellectual independence from elites need not mean independence from the crowd.

author: Aristotle
text: The best limit will probably be, that a more powerful neighbor must have no inducement to go to war with you by reason of the excess of your wealth, but only such as he would have had if you had possessed less.
reference: Politics, Book II · Discussion of Phaleas’s constitution
idea: A community’s wealth can attract attack as well as support its defence. Aristotle treats domestic arrangements and external incentives as connected.

author: Oswald Spengler
work: The Decline of the West, vol. I
text: It will not be—already it is not—permissible to defy clear historical experience and to expect, merely because we hope, that this will spring or that will flourish.
idea: Hope alone does not establish what a civilization can still become. Spengler asks predictions to answer to historical patterns, even when those patterns frustrate our wishes.

author: Diogenes
work: Diogenes Laertius, Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers
text: The musicians fitted the strings to the lyre properly, but left all the habits of their soul ill-arranged.
idea: Technical mastery and self-government are different achievements. The Cynic criticism asks why people carefully maintain their instruments while neglecting their own habits.
note: A saying reported by Diogenes Laertius. Initial connective “That” omitted and first letter capitalized.

author: Democritus
work: Fragments · Source Book in Ancient Philosophy
text: On the contrary, he should have himself so in hand that even when fortune comes his way, and is apparently ready to lead him on to higher things, he should put her aside and not o'erreach his powers.
idea: Good fortune can tempt a person into commitments beyond their capacities. Moderation concerns managing success as well as enduring setbacks.
note: A transmitted ethical saying attributed to Democritus, following advice against undertaking more than one can manage.

author: Isocrates
text: Put yourself in a position in which you have the power to take advantage, but refrain when you have your fair share, so that men may think that you strive for justice, not from weakness, but from a sense of equity.
idea: Restraint is most credible when the person has power to take more. Isocrates distinguishes choosing justice from merely being too weak to exploit another.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Of course I cannot break through the wall by battering my head against it if I really have not the strength to knock it down, but I am not going to be reconciled to it simply because it is a stone wall and I have not the strength.
reference: Notes from Underground, Part I · The stone wall
idea: Acknowledging an unchangeable constraint does not compel emotional agreement with it. The narrator exposes the distance between rational explanation and human willing.
note: The Underground Man speaking; fictional and deliberately unreliable narration.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: The historians, in accord with the old habit of acknowledging divine intervention in human affairs, want to see the cause of events in the expression of the will of someone endowed with power, but that supposition is not confirmed either by reason or by experience.
reference: War and Peace · Second Epilogue, discussion of historical power
idea: Treating a ruler’s will as the sufficient cause of events replaces explanation with a commanding name. Tolstoy asks how power itself is produced.

author: Sophocles
text: But royalty, blest in so much besides, hath the power to do and say what it will.
idea: Antigone identifies an asymmetry between public judgment and what subjects dare say. Authority can control the expression of disagreement without eliminating it.
note: Antigone speaking to Creon in the play; dramatic dialogue.

author: Leonardo da Vinci
work: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci
text: Experience does not err; only your judgments err by expecting from her what is not in her power.
idea: A failed prediction is a reason to examine the judgment imposed on experience. Leonardo separates observation from the expectations the observer brought to it.

author: Marcel Proust
text: Our social personality is created by the thoughts of other people.
idea: Social identity is partly produced by other people’s interpretations. The same person can occupy very different realities in different observers’ minds.
note: The narrator reflecting on the family’s image of Swann. Excerpt from a longer sentence; first letter capitalized.

author: Saint Augustine
text: For that also is a mournful darkness whereby my abilities within me are hidden from me; so that my mind making enquiry into herself of her own powers, ventures not readily to believe herself; because even what is in it is mostly hidden, unless experience reveal it.
reference: Confessions, Book X · Self-knowledge and temptation
idea: Introspection alone does not disclose all our abilities and vulnerabilities. Augustine treats lived tests as revealing what self-examination cannot confidently predict.

author: Saint Augustine
text: Did I wish even by stealth to do contrary to Thy law, because by power I could not, so that being a prisoner, I might mimic a maimed liberty by doing with impunity things unpermitted me, a darkened likeness of Thy Omnipotency?
reference: Confessions, Book II · Reflection on the stolen pears
idea: A forbidden act can be attractive as an imitation of unrestricted power. Augustine examines why violating a rule might matter more to the offender than possessing the stolen object.
note: Augustine questions his own motives; the sentence is not an endorsement of theft.

author: Niccolò Machiavelli
text: Because, if one is on the spot, disorders are seen as they spring up, and one can quickly remedy them; but if one is not at hand, they are heard of only when they are great, and then one can no longer remedy them.
reference: The Prince, chapter III · Mixed principalities
idea: Being present changes how early a ruler detects trouble. Information that reaches a distant authority may arrive only after a cheap remedy is no longer available.

author: Niccolò Machiavelli
text: Because there is no other way of guarding oneself from flatterers except letting men understand that to tell you the truth does not offend you; but when every one may tell you the truth, respect for you abates.
idea: Candour is necessary for sound advice but can conflict with the ruler’s perceived authority. Machiavelli examines how to receive criticism without surrendering command.

author: Edmund Burke
work: Reflections on the Revolution in France
text: The effect of liberty to individuals is, that they may do what they please: we ought to see what it will please them to do, before we risk congratulations, which may be soon turned into complaints.
reference: Reflections on the Revolution in France · Opening discussion of liberty
idea: Burke judges liberty partly through the conduct and institutions it enables. A formal removal of restraints does not, by itself, establish a beneficial outcome.

author: Edmund Burke
work: Reflections on the Revolution in France
text: But as the liberties and the restrictions vary with times and circumstances, and admit of infinite modifications, they cannot be settled upon any abstract rule; and nothing is so foolish as to discuss them upon that principle.
reference: Reflections on the Revolution in France · Civil liberties and restraints
idea: A political principle has to be applied through historically specific circumstances. Burke rejects an abstract formula as a sufficient guide to arranging every liberty and restraint.

author: Alexander Hamilton
text: It is a signal advantage of taxes on articles of consumption, that they contain in their own nature a security against excess.
idea: A tax that suppresses purchases can also reduce the revenue sought. Hamilton identifies a feedback mechanism that limits what an authority can profitably extract.
note: Hamilton’s argument about consumption taxes; not a claim that all such taxes are harmless.

author: Alexander Hamilton
text: The plan offered to our deliberations affects too many particular interests, innovates upon too many local institutions, not to involve in its discussion a variety of objects foreign to its merits, and of views, passions and prejudices little favorable to the discovery of truth.
idea: Debates about institutional reform are affected by the interests that reform will disturb. Hamilton distinguishes a proposal’s merits from the motives shaping discussion of it.

author: François Guizot
work: General History of Civilisation in Europe
translator: Chambers edition (1848); translator unnamed in this edition
text: The theocratical, monarchical, aristocratical, and popular creeds, encounter, struggle with, limit, and modify each other.
reference: Lecture II · Diversity in European civilisation
idea: Competing sources of authority can limit one another before any achieves its ideal form. Guizot explains European development through conflict among institutions, not a single governing principle.

author: François Guizot
work: General History of Civilisation in Europe
translator: Chambers edition (1848); translator unnamed in this edition
text: The more rich and numerous the materials, the more difficult it is to reduce them into a simple and pure form.
reference: Lecture II · Literary form and social diversity
idea: A culture with many competing ideas may produce less formal unity. Guizot connects aesthetic complexity to the diversity of the society supplying its material.

author: Plato
text: Because you fancy that the shepherd or neatherd fattens or tends the sheep or oxen with a view to their own good and not to the good of himself or his master.
reference: Republic, Book I · Thrasymachus on rule
idea: The shepherd image can conceal exploitation behind a language of care. Plato’s dialogue makes the purpose of ruling a contested question, rather than assuming benevolence.
note: Thrasymachus’s challenge to Socrates, not an unqualified statement of Plato’s own conclusion. Excerpt ends at a semicolon in the source.

author: Plato
text: Then, my good friend, I said, do not use compulsion, but let early education be a sort of amusement; you will then be better able to find out the natural bent.
idea: Unforced engagement can reveal aptitudes that obedience conceals. The educational method is also a way of learning about the learner.
note: Socrates speaking in Plato’s dialogue.

author: Albert Camus
text: Myths are made for the imagination to breathe life into them.
reference: Final chapter · Introducing the imagined labour of Sisyphus
idea: Camus makes interpretation an active task. A myth acquires philosophical force when we imagine the experience of the person living it, not merely repeat the plot.

author: Albert Camus
text: But crushing truths perish from being acknowledged.
reference: Final chapter · Consciousness and the tragic hero
idea: Camus suggests that lucid acknowledgement can change our relation to suffering without changing the external facts. The claim concerns the truth’s crushing power, not its factual disappearance.

author: Martin Heidegger
text: Technology is not equivalent to the essence of technology.
idea: Listing devices does not explain the way of understanding that makes them possible. Heidegger separates particular technologies from a broader orientation toward the world.

author: Martin Heidegger
text: Everywhere we remain unfree and chained to technology, whether we passionately affirm or deny it.
idea: Simple enthusiasm and simple rejection can share the same fixation on technology. Heidegger asks for a freer relationship than either reflex allows.

author: Milton Friedman
translator: Original English (1953); Essays in Positive Economics, 1966 printing
text: Observed facts are necessarily finite in number.
reference: The Methodology of Positive Economics · Choosing hypotheses
idea: Evidence underdetermines theory: a limited set of observations can fit many explanations. Friedman therefore asks what else, including new predictions, distinguishes useful hypotheses.
note: Excerpt ends at a semicolon in the source.

author: Milton Friedman
translator: Original English (1953); Essays in Positive Economics, 1966 printing
text: Familiarity with the subject matter of economics breeds contempt for special knowledge about it.
reference: The Methodology of Positive Economics · Conclusion
idea: Everyday participation in an economy can produce unwarranted confidence in explaining it. Friedman distinguishes being familiar with a phenomenon from understanding its causal structure.

author: Karl Popper
translator: Original English (1963); classroom reprint of chapter 1
text: Confirmations should count only if they are the result of risky predictions.
reference: Science: Conjectures and Refutations · Section I, conclusion 2
idea: A result is strong evidence when the theory exposed itself to a plausible failure. Predicting what would surprise a rival account matters more than collecting agreeable examples.
note: Excerpt ends at a semicolon in the source.

author: Karl Popper
translator: Original English (1963); classroom reprint of chapter 1
text: These theories describe some facts, but in the manner of myths.
reference: Science: Conjectures and Refutations · Section II, psychoanalysis
idea: Popper allows that an interpretation can be suggestive while lacking a decisive test. He separates psychological insight from the particular status of a scientific theory.
note: Refers to the Freudian and Adlerian theories discussed in the preceding sentences.

author: Cicero
text: And as to the fact that our school argues against everything, that is only because we could not get a clear view of what is "probable," unless a comparative estimate were made of all the arguments on both sides.
idea: Arguing both sides is a method for estimating probability, not a refusal to judge. Cicero connects intellectual humility with comparative reasoning.

author: Cicero
text: Furthermore, those who wish to be feared must inevitably be afraid of those whom they intimidate.
idea: Coercion creates reciprocal insecurity. A ruler who depends on fear must continually anticipate resistance from those he frightens.

author: Seneca
text: To misuse a benefit like a spendthrift is most shameful, because we do not need our wealth but only our intention to set us free from the obligation of it; for a benefit is repaid by being acknowledged.
idea: Gratitude is not the same transaction as repaying money. Seneca locates its essential obligation in acknowledging goodwill rather than matching the price of a gift.

author: Seneca
text: there can be no God without nature, nor any nature without God; they are both the same thing, differing only in their functions.
idea: In this Stoic account, providence and nature are different names for the order of one reality. Changing the name does not change what sustains us.
note: Continuous clause from Seneca’s explanation of Stoic theology.

author: Johann Gottlieb Fichte
text: When I act, I doubtless know that I act, and how I act; but this knowledge is not the act itself, but only the observation of it.
idea: Observing an action and performing it are different relations to the world. Fichte uses agency to challenge an account of human life confined to representations.

author: Johann Gottlieb Fichte
text: We do not act because we know, but we know because we are called upon to act:—the practical reason is the root of all reason.
idea: Practical commitments give inquiry its direction and significance. Fichte’s claim is about the grounding of knowledge in agency, not permission to ignore evidence.

author: Max Stirner
text: Commoner and laborer believe in the "truth" of money; they who do not possess it believe in it no less than those who possess it: the laymen, therefore, as well as the priests.
reference: Part I · The Free, Political Liberalism; pp. 149–150
idea: An institution’s authority can be sustained by those it disadvantages. Stirner compares shared faith in money with a religious hierarchy.

author: Max Stirner
text: To refuse credit is everybody's affair, and, if a society wants to withdraw it for this or that reason, the man who is hit cannot therefore complain of encroachment on his liberty: the society is simply availing itself of its own liberty.
idea: Freedom to act does not oblige other people to cooperate. Stirner distinguishes social refusal from punishment imposed in the name of a sacred law.

author: Theodor Mommsen
work: The History of Rome, book I
text: So long as the father lived, the persons legally subject to him could never hold property of their own, and therefore could not alienate unless by him so empowered, or yet bequeath.
reference: Book I · chapter V, The Original Constitution of Rome
idea: Economic activity and legal ownership can be separated. Mommsen describes a household structure in which a dependent person’s earnings increased someone else’s estate.

author: Theodor Mommsen
work: The History of Rome, book I
text: As the house-master was not simply the greatest but the only power in the house, so the king was not merely the first but the only holder of power in the state.
reference: Book I · chapter V, The Original Constitution of Rome
idea: Mommsen interprets early kingship through the Roman household: authority is concentrated in one office, even when its functions are delegated. This is his historical reconstruction.

author: Arthur de Gobineau
text: We must not therefore, like the fool in the old adage, wonder at the power of the roseleaf to make the water overflow; we should rather think that the reason of the accident lay in the depths of the water that filled the vessel to overflowing.
reference: Chapter XI · passage on proximate and generating causes
idea: The visible trigger need not explain the scale of an outcome. This passage distinguishes a final disturbance from conditions accumulated beforehand.
note: A causal observation from a work whose racial hierarchy is scientifically discredited; it is not evidence for that hierarchy.

author: Arthur de Gobineau
text: They are themselves influenced in many ways by the local civilization, and cannot succeed in stamping their ideas on a people that fears its conquerors, but is only physically dominated by them.
reference: Chapter IV · discussion of India under British rule
idea: Physical control need not produce cultural agreement. Gobineau uses colonial India to distinguish conquest from assimilation; his general racial theory is scientifically discredited.
note: “They” refers to the English rulers of India; this is Gobineau’s nineteenth-century interpretation.

author: Demosthenes
text: I have told you only what I believe to be expedient for you; and I exhort you not to sacrifice the people of Megalopolis, and to make it your rule, never to sacrifice a smaller power to a greater.
idea: Preserving a weaker state can prevent a stronger neighbor from becoming dominant. The immediate ally’s importance lies partly in the balance it maintains.

author: Demosthenes
text: It was not for their virtue that you once saved the Spartans, nor the Euboeans, that accursed people! nor many others; but because the interests of the city demanded their preservation, as they demanded that of the Phocians just now.
idea: Strategic support need not imply moral admiration. Demosthenes asks his audience to separate an ally’s character from the consequences of abandoning it.

author: François-René de Chateaubriand
text: That is the advantage of being sincere; let every one think what he pleases, provided I am allowed the same liberty; I only endeavour that my opinion shall have the majority, because I think it, and rightly, better than the others.
reference: Volume V · Book XIII, Rome letter dated 28 March 1829
idea: Tolerance can coexist with a conviction that one’s own view is better. Chateaubriand’s hospitality depends on reciprocal freedom, not on agreement.

author: François-René de Chateaubriand
text: When M. de Blacas tells you these tales, he is telling the truth, because he never thwarts the King; but he is not sincere, because he inspires Charles X. only with those wishes which are in accordance with that Prince's inclinations.
reference: Volume V · Book IV, portrait of the Duc de Blacas
idea: An adviser can shape a ruler’s wishes while truthfully denying that he ever opposes them. Chateaubriand distinguishes literal truth from candor about influence.

author: Thomas Carlyle
work: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History
text: The truth of it is embedded in portentous error and falsehood; but the truth of it makes it be believed, not the falsehood: it succeeded by its truth.
reference: Lecture II · The Hero as Prophet
idea: Carlyle attributes the vitality of a belief to the truth he thinks it carries, even when he rejects much of its doctrine. The passage concerns his interpretation of Islam.
note: Carlyle’s nineteenth-century theological judgment, not a neutral description of Islam.

author: Thomas Carlyle
work: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History
text: Liberty of private judgment, if we will consider it, must at all times have existed in the world.
reference: Lecture IV · The Hero as Priest
idea: Carlyle argues that individual judgment operates even inside inherited authority. The Reformation made a permanent human activity explicit rather than inventing it.

author: G. W. F. Hegel
translator: J. B. Baillie; Marxists Internet Archive edition
text: we do not actually and absolutely say what in this sense-certainty we really mean.
idea: Words such as “this” seem to name one unique sensation but can refer to countless objects. Hegel explores the gap between a private intention and the universality of language.
note: Continuous clause; “mean” translates Hegel’s term for intending a particular.

author: G. W. F. Hegel
translator: J. B. Baillie; Marxists Internet Archive edition
text: Both truths have the same authenticity – the immediacy of seeing and the certainty and assurance both have as to their specific way of knowing; but the one certainty disappears in the other.
idea: Two observers can each be immediately certain while pointing to different things. The feeling of direct access therefore cannot by itself resolve their disagreement.

author: Baltasar Gracián
text: Hope is a great falsifier of truth; let skill guard against this by ensuring that fruition exceeds desire.
idea: Expectations change how an outcome is judged. Gracián counsels controlling promises so that a real achievement is not experienced as a disappointment.

author: Baltasar Gracián
text: Things pass for what they seem, not for what they are. Few see inside; many take to the outside.
idea: Public judgment usually has access to appearances rather than inner qualities. Gracián treats making worth legible as a practical problem, without equating appearance with worth.

author: Caesar Augustus
text: a battle or a war ought never to be undertaken, unless the prospect of gain overbalanced the fear of loss.
idea: The decision to fight should compare possible gains with what can be lost, rather than treat victory as intrinsically worthwhile. Suetonius reports this as Augustus’s habitual advice.
note: Suetonius’s report of Augustus’s words, in indirect speech.

author: Caesar Augustus
text: men who pursue small advantages with no small hazard, resemble those who fish with a golden hook, the loss of which, if the line should happen to break, could never be compensated by all the fish they might take.
idea: A profitable-looking opportunity can expose something far more valuable than the reward. The golden hook is a model of disproportionate downside.
note: Suetonius reports this comparison as a saying of Augustus.

author: Thomas Aquinas
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province; Benziger edition
text: For reason in contingent matters may follow opposite courses, as we see in dialectic syllogisms and rhetorical arguments.
reference: Part I · question 83, article 1, I answer that
idea: Aquinas connects freedom to the ability to deliberate between alternatives. Judgments about particular actions do not follow with the necessity of a mathematical demonstration.

author: Thomas Aquinas
translator: Fathers of the English Dominican Province; Benziger edition
text: knowledge is according as the thing known is in the knower, whilst appetite is according as the desirer tends towards the thing desired.
reference: Part I · question 16, article 1, I answer that
idea: Knowing and desiring have different directions: knowledge receives a form of its object, while desire moves toward an object. This distinction underlies Aquinas’s account of truth and goodness.
note: Continuous clause from Aquinas’s own answer, not from an objection.

author: Parmenides
text: It needs must be that what can be thought and spoken of is; for it is possible for it to be, and it is not possible for what is nothing to be.
reference: The Way of Truth · fragment 6 in linked edition (DK B6)
idea: Parmenides makes a radical connection between intelligibility and being: absolute nothingness cannot supply an object of thought. The claim is not that everything imagined physically exists.

author: Parmenides
