text: And, if it came from nothing, what need could have made it arise later rather than sooner?
reference: The Way of Truth · fragment 8 in linked edition (DK B8)
idea: If there were absolutely nothing, no condition could explain why being began at one time rather than another. Parmenides uses this challenge to deny generation from nonbeing.

author: Scipio Africanus
text: I would gladly take her … if I were a private and not a commander.
idea: In this reported refusal of a captive offered to him, Scipio distinguishes private desire from the conduct his office demands. Authority creates obligations that personal appetite does not settle.
note: Plutarch’s reported reply to an offer of a captive woman; ellipsis omits only the narrator’s “said he.”
original: "I would gladly take her," said he, "if I were a private and not a commander."

author: Scipio Africanus
text: he was busiest whenever he had nothing to do.
idea: The anecdote describes Scipio using leisure for literature. The absence of official duties creates room for a different kind of intellectual work.
note: Plutarch’s indirect report of a saying attributed to Scipio.

author: Socrates
text: For the fear of death is indeed the pretence of wisdom, and not real wisdom, being a pretence of knowing the unknown;
idea: Socrates questions the certainty hidden inside fear: treating an unknown outcome as the worst possible one already assumes knowledge. His argument contrasts uncertainty about death with a commitment not to act unjustly.
note: Plato’s portrayal of Socrates; continuous opening clause ending at the source semicolon.

author: Socrates
text: If you think that by killing men you can prevent some one from censuring your evil lives, you are mistaken;
idea: Silencing a critic leaves the grounds for criticism intact. In Plato’s account, Socrates predicts that coercion cannot substitute for changing the conduct being criticized.
note: Plato’s portrayal of Socrates; continuous clause.

author: Pericles
text: Capital, it must be remembered, maintains a war more than forced contributions.
reference: Thucydides · History of the Peloponnesian War, I.141
idea: Stored resources allow a state to sustain operations; repeated demands on citizens become harder to meet. Pericles distinguishes the capacity for one battle from the capacity for a long war.
note: Pericles’s speech as represented by Thucydides.

author: Pericles
text: Farmers are a class of men that are always more ready to serve in person than in purse.
reference: Thucydides · History of the Peloponnesian War, I.141
idea: Pericles argues that willingness to risk one’s body can coexist with reluctance to spend scarce cash. The form of a society’s resources shapes how it can fight.
note: Pericles’s assessment of the Peloponnesians, as represented by Thucydides; not a universal finding about farmers.

author: Tacitus
translator: Revised Oxford translation, edition introduced by Edward Brooks, Jr.
text: their generals command less through the force of authority, than of example.
idea: Tacitus describes a form of command sustained by visible courage rather than unlimited office. His portrait of Germanic customs also invites comparison with Roman power.
note: Continuous clause; historical interpretation by a Roman observer.

author: Tacitus
translator: Revised Oxford translation, edition introduced by Edward Brooks, Jr.
text: With language we should have lost memory itself, had it been as much in our power to forget, as to be silent.
idea: Suppression can stop public speech more easily than it can erase experience. Tacitus links political freedom to the preservation and transmission of memory.

author: Voltaire
text: In fine, men, generally going with the stream, seldom judge for themselves, and purity of taste is almost as rare as talent.
idea: A reputation can persist because people inherit one another’s judgments. Voltaire asks readers to distinguish excellence from accumulated approval.

author: Voltaire
text: For the same reason the Sadducees were permitted not to believe in the angels, although the angels are so often spoken of in the Old Testament; but these same Sadducees were not permitted to neglect the prescribed feasts, fasts, and ceremonies.
idea: Voltaire distinguishes required practices from permitted differences of belief. In his historical argument, a shared institution need not rest on uniform assent to every story.
note: Voltaire’s historical interpretation; included as an example of his reasoning, not as a settled account of ancient Judaism.

author: Aristophanes
text: How, then, if justice exists, has Jupiter not perished, who bound his own father?
reference: The Clouds · debate of Just Cause and Unjust Cause
idea: The Unjust Cause uses a god’s misconduct to attack an appeal to divine justice. The comedy exposes how a tradition’s own examples can be turned against its moral authority.
note: Spoken by Unjust Cause in a comic debate; not Aristophanes asserting that injustice is right.

author: Aristophanes
text: But what if, having the worst Cause, I shall conquer you in arguing, proving that it is right to beat one’s mother?
reference: The Clouds · Phidippides’s argument with Strepsiades
idea: An argumentative technique taught for personal advantage can be turned against its sponsor. The father’s project of evading obligations returns as a justification for harming his own family.
note: Spoken by Phidippides; the play dramatizes the destructive result of treating victory as proof.

author: Cyrus the Great
text: To seize it may be the fruit of daring and daring only, but to hold it is impossible without self-restraint and self-command and endless care.
idea: Conquest and durable government demand different capacities. Xenophon’s Cyrus warns that the boldness which wins an empire cannot by itself preserve it.
note: “It” refers to empire; spoken by Cyrus in Xenophon’s literary portrait.

author: Cyrus the Great
text: the more a man possesses, the more there are to envy him, to plot against him, and be his enemies, above all when the wealth he wins and the services he receives are yielded by reluctant hands.
idea: An accumulation of power can also accumulate hostility. Xenophon makes the maintenance of empire especially demanding when compliance is unwilling.
note: Continuous clause from Cyrus’s speech in Xenophon’s literary portrait.

author: Dante Alighieri
text: Not because more than one unmingled semblance Was in the living light on which I looked, For it is always what it was before; But through the sight, that fortified itself In me by looking, one appearance only To me was ever changing as I changed.
idea: The object of vision need not change for understanding to deepen. Dante describes his own capacity to see being transformed by sustained attention.

author: Dante Alighieri
text: Hence, if the present world doth go astray, In you the cause is, be it sought in you;
idea: Marco rejects the excuse that the heavens determine every human action. Moral and political failure remain matters for human responsibility.
note: Marco Lombardo speaking to Dante; continuous clause.

author: Desiderius Erasmus
text: For by the same reason he would call the warlike horse unfortunate, because he understood not grammar, nor ate cheese-cakes; and the bull miserable, because he'd make so ill a wrestler.
reference: Folly’s speech · the natural condition of human beings
idea: A judgment of deficiency can smuggle in an unsuitable standard. Folly ridicules measuring one kind of creature by capacities belonging to another.
note: Spoken by the personified Folly; a satirical challenge, not a literal rejection of learning.

author: Desiderius Erasmus
text: And yet this is found by experience among my fools, that not only truths but even open reproaches are heard with pleasure; so that the same thing which, if it came from a wise man's mouth might prove a capital crime, spoken by a fool is received with delight.
reference: Folly’s speech · fools at the courts of princes
idea: The social role of a speaker changes what can safely be said. A joke may deliver criticism that would be punished as a serious assertion.
note: Spoken by Folly in Erasmus’s satire.

author: Euripides
text: Art learning only now, that every single man cares for himself more than for his neighbour, some from honest motives, others for mere gain's sake?
idea: The Attendant distinguishes self-concern from its motives: similar conduct can be justified as duty or pursued for gain. His cynical generalization frames Jason’s abandonment of his family.
note: A character’s judgment, not an empirical law about every person.

author: Euripides
text: Strange are the tempers of princes, and maybe because they seldom have to obey, and mostly lord it over others, change they their moods with difficulty.
idea: Habitual command can weaken the ability to yield. The Nurse connects princely inflexibility with a life in which other people do the adjusting.
note: Spoken by the Nurse.

author: Homer
text: the gods do not grace all men alike in speech, person, and understanding.
reference: Odyssey · Book VIII, Ulysses answers Euryalus
idea: Visible impressiveness does not guarantee judgment or eloquence. Ulysses rebukes a handsome athlete for mistaking appearance for a complete measure of ability.
note: Ulysses speaking in the poem, in Samuel Butler’s translation.

author: Homer
text: Jove takes half the goodness out of a man when he makes a slave of him.
reference: Odyssey · Book XVII, Eumaeus on servitude
idea: Eumaeus presents enslavement as something that diminishes a person’s capacities. The remark connects conduct to a loss of freedom rather than treating servility as an inborn quality.
note: Spoken by Eumaeus, who is himself enslaved; “goodness” is Butler’s rendering.

author: Horace
translator: Christopher Smart; revised by Theodore Alois Buckley
text: I am disgusted that any thing should be found fault with, not because it is a lumpish composition or inelegant, but because it is modern; and that not a favorable allowance, but honor and rewards are demanded for the old writers.
reference: Epistles · Book II, Epistle I, to Augustus
idea: Antiquity can become an unearned credential. Horace objects to a double standard that excuses older writers while treating novelty itself as a defect.

author: Horace
translator: Christopher Smart; revised by Theodore Alois Buckley
text: Many brave men lived before Agamemnon: but all of them, unlamented and unknown, are overwhelmed with endless obscurity, because they were destitute of a sacred bard.
reference: Odes · Book IV, Ode IX, to Lollius
idea: Historical remembrance depends on representation as well as achievement. Horace gives poetry a role in determining which acts remain visible to later generations.

author: Julius Caesar
text: all men likewise, by nature, love liberty and hate the condition of slavery,
idea: Caesar recognizes the motive behind resistance even as he organizes its suppression. Understanding an opponent’s desire does not imply endorsing its political success.
note: Continuous clause from Caesar’s explanation of the Gallic coalition.

author: Julius Caesar
text: the price of provisions was raised, which is commonly a disaster attendant, not only on a time of present scarcity, but on the apprehension of future want.
idea: Expectations can alter present conditions: anticipated shortage raises prices before supplies are fully exhausted. Caesar describes this mechanism during the Ilerda campaign.
note: Continuous clause from Caesar’s account.

author: Plutarch
translator: John Dryden translation, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough (1859)
text: sometimes a matter of less moment, an expression or a jest, informs us better of their characters and inclinations, than the most famous sieges, the greatest armaments, or the bloodiest battles whatsoever.
idea: A small, less guarded action can reveal motives that a public achievement conceals. Plutarch explains why biography selects different evidence from military history.
note: Continuous clause from the prologue.

author: Plutarch
translator: John Dryden translation, revised by Arthur Hugh Clough (1859)
text: For my part, I assure you, I had rather excel others in the knowledge of what is excellent, than in the extent of my power and dominion.
reference: Life of Alexander · §7, letter to Aristotle
idea: The reported letter treats knowledge as a source of distinction that political power cannot replace. Alexander complains that publishing the teaching makes this advantage available to others.
note: Alexander’s words in a letter reported by Plutarch; not Plutarch speaking in his own voice.

author: Virgil
text: Tho’ plung’d by Fortune’s pow’r in misery, ’Tis not in Fortune’s pow’r to make me lie.
idea: A claim to moral independence can be used to win trust. Sinon’s statement is deceptive; Virgil shows how the performance of integrity can make a false story persuasive.
note: Spoken by Sinon, whose deceit helps bring the wooden horse into Troy.

author: Virgil
text: What Diomede, nor Thetis’ greater son, A thousand ships, nor ten years’ siege, had done: False tears and fawning words the city won.
reference: Aeneid · Book II, Aeneas recounts Sinon’s deception
idea: Troy resists military force but falls when its judgment is manipulated. The passage contrasts the strength of defenses with the vulnerability of the beliefs directing them.
note: Aeneas narrating the fall of Troy.

author: William Shakespeare
text: The jewel that we find, we stoop and take ’t, Because we see it; but what we do not see, We tread upon, and never think of it.
reference: Measure for Measure · Act II, scene 1, Angelo
idea: Enforcement depends on what becomes visible to authorities. Angelo argues that undiscovered wrongdoing does not excuse a discovered offense; his own later behavior complicates this confidence.

author: William Shakespeare
text: Spirits are not finely touched But to fine issues; nor nature never lends The smallest scruple of her excellence But, like a thrifty goddess, she determines Herself the glory of a creditor, Both thanks and use.
reference: Measure for Measure · Act I, scene 1, the Duke
idea: A gift of ability creates an obligation to use it for others. The Duke treats personal excellence as a loan owed back to the world, while appointing Angelo to govern.

author: Arnold J. Toynbee
translator: English; challenge-and-response excerpt reproduced by Panarchy
text: Is there such a thing as an excessive challenge?
reference: The Challenge Hypothesis · discussion of limits
idea: Toynbee asks whether adversity stops being productive beyond a threshold. His account distinguishes a stimulus that elicits invention from a burden that overwhelms a society.

author: Arnold J. Toynbee
translator: English; challenge-and-response excerpt reproduced by Panarchy
text: Extreme in degree though these three challenges are, they are limited in range
reference: The Challenge Hypothesis · Venice, Holland and Switzerland
idea: A harsh physical environment can also protect a society from invasion. Toynbee warns against treating difficulty in one dimension as difficulty in every dimension.
note: Continuous opening clause; the three cases are Venice, Holland and Switzerland.

author: Arthur C. Clarke
work: The Light of Other Days · with Stephen Baxter
text: history has never been a simple record of the past, but a means of shaping peoples.
reference: The Light of Other Days · extract reproduced by the Clarke Foundation
idea: The novel treats historical memory as active in forming collective identities. Recording what happened and organizing what a people understands itself to be are intertwined.
note: Continuous clause from the coauthored novel, not a statement uniquely attributable to Clarke.

author: Arthur C. Clarke
work: The Light of Other Days · with Stephen Baxter
text: the equilibrium state of the cosmos is death
reference: The Light of Other Days · extract reproduced by the Clarke Foundation
idea: The novel’s pessimistic reflection contrasts living organization with cosmic equilibrium. It raises the question of how fragile local life can matter in a universe indifferent to its survival.
note: Clause from a speculative reflection in the coauthored novel; not a scientific proof or a statement uniquely attributable to Clarke.

author: Ayn Rand
text: All definitions are contextual, and a primitive definition does not contradict a more advanced one: the latter merely expands the former.
idea: A definition can be valid at an earlier level of knowledge and later become more precise. Rand distinguishes expanding a concept from contradicting what was already established.

author: Ayn Rand
text: Man retains his concepts by means of language.
reference: “The Psycho-Epistemology of Art” · The Romantic Manifesto, p. 17
idea: Words let a person retain conceptual groupings larger than immediate perception can hold. In this account language supports the storage and reuse of abstractions.

author: Carl Schmitt
translator: George Schwab (1985; University of Chicago Press edition 2005)
text: The exception is more interesting than the rule.
idea: A breakdown can expose the decisions on which normal legal order depends. Schmitt treats exceptional cases as evidence about authority that routine compliance conceals.

author: Carl Schmitt
translator: George Schwab (1985; University of Chicago Press edition 2005)
text: The decision frees itself from all normative ties and becomes in the true sense absolute.
idea: Schmitt’s account separates the decision to preserve a state from the norms it suspends. This identifies the danger, as well as the claimed force, of sovereignty in an emergency.
note: Schmitt’s theory of the exception, not a recommendation to remove legal constraints.

author: Emil Cioran
translator: Richard Howard; Penguin publisher sample (2020 edition)
text: For every discomfort is only an abortive metaphysical experience.
reference: Chapter I · printed p. 9, paragraph on revelation and discomfort
idea: Cioran imagines ordinary unease as an experience that almost becomes a revelation about existence. The aphorism dramatizes a possible relation between mood and philosophy.

author: Emil Cioran
translator: Richard Howard; Penguin publisher sample (2020 edition)
text: Lucidity is the only vice which makes us free – free in a desert.
idea: Seeing through consoling illusions can free a person while also stripping the world of attachment and purpose. Cioran makes liberation and desolation arrive together.

author: Ernst Jünger
text: The decision then falls to the individual,
reference: The Forest Passage · chapter 31, publisher-authorized excerpt
idea: When institutions themselves become instruments of oppression, obedience no longer settles the moral question. Jünger places responsibility back on the person confronting the demand.
note: Continuous clause; “then” refers to the corruption of institutions described in the preceding paragraph.

author: Ernst Jünger
text: This indicates how far the law has become dubious.
reference: The Forest Passage · chapter 31, publisher-authorized excerpt
idea: Jünger reads fascination with literary criminals as a symptom of lost confidence in law. The diagnosis concerns legitimacy; it does not make criminals automatically admirable.
note: “This” refers to the prominence of criminals in the literature he is discussing.

author: Franz Kafka
text: My being innocent does not make things simple,
reference: The Trial · chapter 7, K. speaking to Titorelli
idea: Being innocent and being able to establish innocence are different problems. Kafka places K. inside a procedure whose operation is not controlled by the fact he wants it to recognize.
note: K.’s reply; the source continues with the narrator’s speech attribution.

author: Franz Kafka
text: No documents ever get lost, the court forgets nothing.
reference: The Trial · chapter 7, Titorelli on apparent acquittal
idea: An apparently finished case can remain available for reactivation. Titorelli describes an institutional memory that preserves power over someone even during a period of freedom.
note: Titorelli speaking within the novel.

author: Friedrich Hayek
work: The Use of Knowledge in Society
text: scientific knowledge is not the sum of all knowledge.
reference: Section III · kinds of socially relevant knowledge
idea: Formal expertise does not exhaust what matters for coordination. Hayek emphasizes practical knowledge of local circumstances that is often difficult to collect centrally.

author: Friedrich Hayek
work: The Use of Knowledge in Society
text: economic problems arise always and only in consequence of change.
idea: Allocation requires repeated revision because circumstances change. Hayek is arguing about the need for adjustment, not denying the existence of scarcity.

author: George Orwell
text: The great enemy of clear language is insincerity.
reference: Politics and the English Language · paragraph on declared and actual aims
idea: When a writer’s purpose cannot be candidly stated, vague language becomes useful. Orwell connects obscurity with the incentive to conceal a gap between words and intentions.

author: George Orwell
text: Orthodoxy, of whatever colour, seems to demand a lifeless, imitative style.
reference: Politics and the English Language · discussion of the party line
idea: Ready-made loyalty can produce ready-made prose. Orwell treats imitation of language as one way a political group discourages independent thought.

author: Karl Jaspers
translator: English excerpt in Walter Kaufmann’s edited anthology; translator not identified on linked page
text: The content of our truth depends upon our appropriating the historical foundation.
idea: Inherited thought becomes philosophically useful through active appropriation. Jaspers distinguishes working through a tradition from merely repeating its conclusions.

author: Karl Jaspers
translator: English excerpt in Walter Kaufmann’s edited anthology; translator not identified on linked page
text: Only as an individual can man become a philosopher.
reference: On My Philosophy · discussion of philosophy and institutions
idea: An institution can teach ideas but cannot perform another person’s philosophical commitment. Jaspers locates this responsibility in the learner rather than in a credential or school.

author: Leo Strauss
text: liberal education cannot be simply indoctrination.
reference: What Is Liberal Education? · paragraph on disagreement among great thinkers
idea: The authors worth studying disagree on central questions. Strauss argues that serious engagement with them therefore requires judgment rather than passive acceptance.
note: Continuous concluding clause.

author: Leo Strauss
text: whereas the gentleman must be wealthy in order to do his proper work, the philosopher may be poor.
reference: Liberal Education and Responsibility · excerpt on the gentleman and the philosopher
idea: Strauss distinguishes the leisure and social standing of the traditional gentleman from the conditions of philosophical inquiry. Socrates supplies his example of thought independent of wealth.
note: A clause within Strauss’s comparison of classical social and philosophical ideals.

author: Ludwig von Mises
text: But society is nothing but the combination of individuals for cooperative effort.
idea: Mises resists treating society as a separate person with an independent will. Collective outcomes must be explained through the actions and cooperation of individuals.

author: Ludwig von Mises
text: The category end makes sense only when applied to action.
idea: Purposes belong to acting agents. Mises warns against assigning a goal to a collective abstraction without explaining whose actions pursue it.

author: Nick Land
translator: Original English; Urbanomic publisher excerpt (2011 edition)
text: As markets learn to manufacture intelligence, politics modernizes, upgrades paranoia, and tries to get a grip…
idea: Land imagines technical development as an increasingly autonomous process to which politics reacts. The formulation puts adaptation and control into tension.
note: Speculative philosophical prose; this is Land’s model, not an established forecast.

author: Nick Land
work: Odds and Ends: On Ultimate Risk
text: Only then does risk become ‘existential’, absolute, or transcendental, fully subsuming the gambler into the game, and the game into itself.
reference: Odds and Ends: On Ultimate Risk · opening excerpt, Collapse VIII, pp. 361–384
idea: Ordinary gambling risks a stake while leaving the game intact. Land asks what changes when the survival of the whole system—and the gambler—is itself at stake.
note: “Then” refers to the preceding image of the casino itself becoming the stake.

author: Slavoj Žižek
work: Some Bewildered Clarifications: A Response to Noam Chomsky
text: no effective ideology simply lies:
reference: Some Bewildered Clarifications · paragraph beginning “My underlying thesis”
idea: Žižek argues that ideology leaves traces of the reality it conceals in its own inconsistencies. Criticism can examine the account’s form as well as checking its factual claims.
note: Continuous clause; the colon introduces his explanation.

author: Slavoj Žižek
work: Some Bewildered Clarifications: A Response to Noam Chomsky
text: as if it is the very outrage at suffering which turns us into its immobilized fascinated spectators.
reference: Some Bewildered Clarifications · paragraph on reported suffering
idea: Moral outrage can become a way of watching that substitutes for action. Žižek raises this as a possibility about spectatorship, not as a reason to disregard suffering.
note: Continuous conjectural clause from the essay.

author: Edward Gibbon
work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
text: His haughty and inflexible spirit could not discover, or would not acknowledge, the advantage of preserving an intermediate power, however imaginary, between the emperor and the army.
reference: Chapter V · Septimius Severus and the senate
idea: An institution can mediate power even when its authority is partly ceremonial. Gibbon argues that Severus’s contempt for the senate removed a buffer between the ruler and military force.
note: Gibbon’s historical interpretation of Septimius Severus.

author: Edward Gibbon
work: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
text: The successors of Augustus exercised the power of dictating whatever laws their wisdom or caprice might suggest; but those laws were ratified by the sanction of the senate.
reference: Chapter XIII · Diocletian, Maximian and the declining senate
idea: Legal forms can survive after substantive control has shifted. Gibbon also suggests that maintaining those forms can still constrain the language and behavior of rulers.

author: Fernando Pessoa
text: And I carry other people within me.
reference: The Book of Disquiet · fragment beginning “Conviver com os outros é uma tortura para mim”
idea: Physical solitude does not remove an imagined audience. The narrator carries other people’s possible judgments into his own experience of himself.
original: E eu tenho os outros em mim.
note: Bernardo Soares, Pessoa’s literary narrator; the linked edition organizes the fragments by their opening words.

author: Giambattista Vico
translator: Marginalia editorial translation from Italian (1744 text; Nicolini edition, 1928)
text: In children memory is extremely vigorous; hence imagination is excessively vivid, being nothing other than memory expanded or combined.
reference: The New Science · Book I, axiom L, §211
idea: Vico describes imagination as a recombination and enlargement of memory. He uses childhood as a model for understanding the image-making cultures of early humanity.
original: Ne’ fanciulli è vigorosissima la memoria; quindi vivida all’eccesso la fantasia, ch’altro non è che memoria o dilatata o composta.

author: Giambattista Vico
translator: Marginalia editorial translation from Italian (1744 text; Nicolini edition, 1928)
text: For the arts are nothing but imitations of nature and, in a certain way, real poems.
idea: Vico places practical invention before philosophical explanation. The “arts” here include useful skills: making things can embody a poetic grasp of nature before it becomes an abstract theory.
original: perché l’arti non sono altro ch’imitazioni della natura e poesie in un certo modo reali.
note: Continuous final clause of §217.

author: Max Weber
translator: Allison L. Hurst (2018), adapted from Gerth and Mills (1946)
text: To be sure, the pure types are rarely found in reality.
reference: Politics as a Vocation · discussion of types of legitimate domination
idea: Traditional, charismatic and legal authority are analytical distinctions. Weber warns against expecting actual institutions to fit one category without mixture.
note: University teaching edition, CC BY-SA 4.0; adapted translation, not the unmodified Gerth–Mills text.

author: Max Weber
translator: Allison L. Hurst (2018), adapted from Gerth and Mills (1946)
text: Either one lives for politics or one lives off politics.
reference: Politics as a Vocation · professional politicians
idea: Weber immediately says these categories can overlap. The distinction raises a practical issue: restricting politics to unpaid service favors people who already have independent wealth.
note: University teaching edition, CC BY-SA 4.0; the contrast is explicitly not exclusive.

author: Montesquieu
translator: Marginalia editorial translation from French; Laboulaye edition
text: When the judge presumes, judgments become arbitrary; when the law presumes, it gives the judge a fixed rule.
reference: The Spirit of Laws · Book XXIX, chapter 16
idea: A presumption stated in advance differs from an inference improvised by an official. Montesquieu connects predictable legal standards with limits on discretion.
original: Lorsque le juge présume, les jugements deviennent arbitraires [1] ; lorsque la loi présume, elle donne au juge une règle fixe.
note: The source’s footnote marker is omitted from the English quotation.

author: Montesquieu
translator: Marginalia editorial translation from French; Laboulaye edition
text: A law must have its effect, and departure from it must not be permitted by a private agreement.
reference: The Spirit of Laws · Book XXIX, chapter 16
idea: A rule may defeat itself if private parties can simply contract around the protection it was meant to establish. Montesquieu illustrates this with Roman inheritance law.
original: Une loi doit avoir son effet, et il ne faut pas permettre d’y déroger par une convention particulière.

author: Nicolae Steinhardt
work: Dăruind vei dobândi (Giving, You Shall Receive)
text: Dare to give what, for a time, you happen to lack.
reference: Dăruind vei dobândi · closing discussion of monastic life
idea: Steinhardt treats encouragement and faith as capacities that can grow through giving them to another person. The paradox challenges the assumption that one must first feel inwardly complete.
original: sa indraznesti a da ceea ce vremelnic se intampla sa-ti lipseasca.
note: Clause from the sermon’s account of monastic life.

author: Nicolae Steinhardt
work: Dăruind vei dobândi (Giving, You Shall Receive)
text: through an excess of happiness and moments of euphoria
reference: Dăruind vei dobândi · discussion of Camus on Oscar Wilde
idea: Steinhardt allows joy, as well as suffering, to become a path toward Christ. His reading resists reducing spiritual depth to pain alone.
original: ci prin exces de fericire si in clipe de euforie
note: A continuous phrase from Steinhardt’s reflection on Camus; not a direct quotation of Camus.

author: Ovid
text: His hoariness is still the same, the same violence appears in his features; his eyes are bright as before; he is still the same image of ferocity.
idea: The change into a wolf reveals a violence already present in the man. Ovid makes bodily transformation preserve and expose character rather than erase identity.
note: The narrator describes Lycaon after Jupiter transforms him.

author: Ovid
text: But a new power draws me on, against my will; and Cupid persuades one thing, reason another.
reference: Metamorphoses · Book VII, Medea’s opening soliloquy
idea: Recognizing a reason and being moved by it are different achievements. Medea experiences desire as a rival source of persuasion inside her own deliberation.
note: Medea speaking in Ovid’s poem.

author: Stendhal
translator: Philip Sidney Woolf and Cecil N. Sidney Woolf (1915; linked 1920 edition)
text: A man who is all-powerful relishes only one sort of advice, the advice of those that tell him to increase his power.
reference: On Love · Book II, chapter LIV, Of the Education of Women
idea: Power can distort the advice a person welcomes. Stendhal applies the analogy of despotism to men’s resistance to changing women’s education.

author: Stendhal
translator: Philip Sidney Woolf and Cecil N. Sidney Woolf (1915; linked 1920 edition)
text: Power is, after love, the first source of happiness, only because one believes oneself to be in a position to command sympathy.
reference: On Love · author’s note on power and sympathy
idea: For Stendhal, attraction to power can depend on a wish for other people’s sympathy. The explanation also exposes a tension: commanded attention may fail to supply the affection being sought.

author: Søren Kierkegaard
translator: Lee M. Hollander (1923), in Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard
text: As far as I am concerned, I am able to describe most excellently the movements of faith; but I cannot make them myself.
idea: Describing a commitment is not the same as being able to live it. The pseudonymous speaker makes the distance between conceptual understanding and existential participation explicit.
note: Johannes de silentio, Kierkegaard’s pseudonymous narrator.

author: Søren Kierkegaard
work: Preparation for a Christian Life (Practice in Christianity)
translator: Lee M. Hollander (1923), in Selections from the Writings of Kierkegaard
text: But faith in its own right protests against every attempt to approach Jesus Christ by the help of historical information about the consequences of his life.
reference: Preparation for a Christian Life · discussion of Christ and historical results
idea: The authority of Christianity cannot, in this account, be inferred simply from its later success. The reader is asked to face the original demand of faith without the reassurance of hindsight.
note: Anti-Climacus, Kierkegaard’s pseudonymous author; Hollander’s selection uses this English title.

author: Xenophon
text: If so, what is the difference between depreciating obedience to law because laws will be repealed, and depreciating good discipline in war because peace will one day be made?
reference: Memorabilia · Book IV, chapter IV, Socrates and Hippias
idea: That a rule may later change does not by itself remove its present function. Xenophon’s Socrates challenges the inference from mutability to worthlessness.
note: Socrates speaking in Xenophon’s account.

author: Xenophon
text: Where then is the difficulty of supposing that a man may be temperate to-day, and to-morrow the reverse; or that he who once has had it in his power to act virtuously may not quite lose that power?
idea: Virtue is a capacity that can deteriorate when practice and circumstances change. Xenophon uses this to question whether a pupil’s later wrongdoing disproves the value of earlier teaching.
